To quantify a GI score, we first defined the degree to which pairs of sgRNAs deviated from expectations using an additive model of L2FC (which is equivalent to a multiplicative model in linear space)83. Single-targeting pairs, in which a targeting sgRNA is paired with a non-targeting control, are used to determine the fitness effect of knocking down a particular gene. Expected effects of knocking down two genes are therefore taken as the sum of individual effects:

where \(\text{L2FC}(G|{g}_{1}=a,{g}_{2}=b)\) represents the L2FC predicted by the Bayesian two-line model at generation G for a given pair of guides, a and b, at sgRNA positions 1 and 2, respectively, and NT represents the non-targeting controls. Deviations from expectations are then defined as follows:

To summarize the deviations to a single value, we define ΔL2FC as the deviation from expectations at G = 25.

To address the possibility of a floor effect84 (cases in which the expected phenotype exceeds the maximal fitness cost that can be accurately detected in our experiment), a generalized additive model (GAM)85 was fitted using the bam function from the mgcv package (v.1.9-3) in R (v.4.3.1) to correct the observed deviations. Deviations were modelled as:

where \(\hat{s}\) is the penalized regression spline GAM (with k = 20, method = “ML”, scaled t-distribution family). By modelling deviations in this manner, the penalized smoothing encourages predictions to follow the observed trend in data-sparse regions (that is, a near-linear continuation of the observed versus expected relationship), effectively reducing abrupt changes in deviations when there is little data to support them. The final, corrected, deviations were thus calculated as:

Finally, the GI score for a pair of genes A and B was summarized as the median of the Δ′ for all of the guide pairs targeting those genes; that is,

A Bayesian mixture model was used to identify statistically significant interactions. The mixture consisted of two distributions: a normal distribution representing the null hypothesis of no interaction with a prior mean of 0, and a uniform distribution representing the alternative hypothesis. The posterior probability of a GI score belonging to the alternative hypothesis was calculated, and interactions were classified as likely interactions if the posterior probability was greater than 0.5, and as confident interactions if the posterior probability was greater than 0.95. We use a cut-off of 0.5 for likely interactions because this corresponds to the point at which GI scores are more likely to be explained by the uniform distribution than by the normal distribution.

To integrate the evidence from the two independent Mtb screens (experiment 1 and experiment 2) into a single, directly interpretable probability, a joint Bayesian mixture model was fitted to the paired GI scores. For each gene pair, the GI score in each experiment and its standard error (that is, mean GI score and the standard deviation of Δ′ from the Bayesian two-line model) were taken as the x,y coordinates and their measurement uncertainties.

The mixture consisted of five components defined over the range of GI scores: a null component and four interaction components, one for each quadrant. The null hypothesis of no interaction was represented by a bivariate normal distribution centred near the origin, with a correlation parameter, ρ, given a weakly informative prior centred at zero. Allowing ρ to be a free parameter allowed the model to learn any existing correlation observed in the null distribution, owing to each screen using the same library and protocols. Per-pair measurement error was incorporated into the null by adding each pair’s squared standard error to the variance on the corresponding axis and scaling ρ accordingly (see Stan model code for implementation details). This approach incorporates the uncertainty associated with each GI-score estimate, down-weighting imprecise measurements while integrating both the consistency and the precision of observed effects across the two screens.

The four interaction components corresponded to the concordant negative quadrant, the concordant positive quadrant and the two discordant quadrants in which the two experiments disagreed in sign (one positive and the other negative). Each quadrant was modelled as a product of per-axis uniform densities over the range of observed scores, which were winsorized at the 0.1st and 99.9th percentiles to reduce the influence of outliers. Because pairs near a quadrant edge could belong to a neighbouring quadrant owing to measurement uncertainty, the uniform densities were convolved with the per-pair measurement error at the origin. Thus, a pair lying near an axis is assigned partly to each quadrant, and the model identifies the most likely membership from the mixture. The mixture weights were given a Dirichlet(2, 2, 36) prior over the concordant, discordant and null components, placing an 18-fold higher weight on the null, reflecting the expectation that most gene pairs do not interact. Concordant and discordant weights were divided evenly between their two respective quadrants (two discordant quadrants and the concordant positive and concordant negative quadrants). The model was fitted using Stan (cmdstan v.2.35, cmdstanpy v.1.2.4). For each gene pair, the posterior probability of belonging to each component was computed and summarized as the probability of a negative, positive or discordant interaction, and of no interaction. As in the single-experiment analysis, a pair was classified as a likely interaction when the largest of its interaction-class probabilities exceeded 0.5 and as a confident interaction when it exceeded 0.95, and was labelled negative, positive or discordant according to the dominant class.

To explore patterns of similarity in GI profiles, the GI matrix was hierarchically clustered using average linkage with Pearson correlation as the similarity measure, as implemented in SciPy86. At each internal node of the clustering hierarchy, the descendant genes were tested for Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment using GOATOOLS87. GO annotations were obtained from UniProt and mapped to the go-basic ontology, with the full set of genes in the GI map used as the background. Enrichment P values were calculated using Fisher’s exact test and corrected for multiple-hypothesis testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Nodes were designated as key nodes when they represented the most significant occurrence (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.005) for at least one biological process term. Each key node was labelled with its most significant GO term, and a GO-DAG specificity constraint was enforced such that no parent node carried a more specific term than its descendants. To reduce redundancy, key nodes with highly overlapping parent gene sets (Jaccard ≥ 0.8) were removed. Distinct colours were assigned to the remaining key nodes and propagated through their descendant branches, producing functionally labelled dendrograms in which leaves inherited the most specific term in their lineage.

Pathways were defined using a combination of KEGG and PATRIC pathways together with manual curation (Supplementary Table 4). Genes were assigned to pathways on the basis of manual curation and AI-assisted literature review (Claude Sonnet 4.5). Gene pairs were categorized as having a significant GI (p > 0.5) or not, and Fisher’s exact test was used to assess the association between pathway pairs and significant GIs. Self-interactions, in which a gene is targeted twice (that is, A + A), were excluded from the analysis. The resulting P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. The analysis was performed twice: once using all gene pairs and once excluding potential polar effects (defined as pairs in which the genes were five genes or fewer apart), to assess how significance changed.

Sequences for selected genes were co-folded with AlphaFold-Multimer28 (v.3) to predict protein complex structures and AlphaFold34 to predict PPIs. All model inputs for Mtb used amino acid sequences from the H37Rv reference proteome (UniProt: UP000001584). All model inputs for Msm used amino acid sequences translated using BioPython from strain mc2155 (RefSeq: NC_008596.1), with the following exceptions. MSMEG5414 in the reference genome was split into proteins MSMEG5414A and MSMEG5414B. Four genes are misannotated in the reference genome as pseudogenes, and their translations were manually included: MSMEG4629:folC and MSMEG1828 from another genome (GenBank: CP009494); MSMEG1843:ahcY from UniProt (accession A4ZHR8); and MSMEG1400:fusA1 from a previously reported sequence88,89. All sequence inputs for Msm can be found in the file msm_essential_proteome.fa in our linked GitHub repository (see ‘Code availability’). AlphaFold-Multimer inputs were formatted as pairs of monomers28. These complexes were predicted using LocalColabFold90 v.1.5.5 (https://github.com/YoshitakaMo/localcolabfold)90 on an NVIDIA L40S GPU and 16 24-GB CPUs. The model was run with three recycles and AMBER relaxation. AlphaFold3 inputs were prepared following a modified pooled AlphaFold3 approach27. Within the bin-packing strategy, smaller protein sequences were prioritized to maximize the number of monomers per pool. In both cases, five predicted structures were generated per input. Predicted TM scores (pTMs) and interface predicted TM scores (ipTMs) for any given gene or gene pair, respectively, were taken as a mean across all models. ipTMs were corrected for combined protein length as previously described27. In Supplementary Tables 2 and 3, columns from pooled inputs on the web server have the suffix or infix ‘_webserver’.

Structures and scores were also generated locally for Mtb using the same pooled inputs as the AlphaFold3 web server. Per-chain multiple sequence alignments were generated with ColabFold v.1.5.590 using MMseqs2 18.8cc5c91 against the UniRef30 (2023-02) and ColabFold environmental clusters (2021-08; comprising filtered BFD, MGnify, MetaEuk and SMAG sub-databases), with GPU-accelerated prefiltering (--gpu 1 --prefilter-mode 1). The output was written directly in AlphaFold3-compatible JSON form (--af3-json), yielding one unpaired multiple sequence alignment per chain. To avoid recomputing identical alignments across the many overlapping pools in this study, sequences were keyed by SHA-256 hash and computed only once; an indexed central cache of all previously generated alignments (about 3,800 unique sequences) was consulted on every job, with cache hits delivering byte-identical multiple sequence alignments and cache misses triggering a fresh ColabFold run that subsequently updated the cache. Co-folding was performed with AlphaFold3 v.3.0.14 executed inside an Apptainer/Singularity container on NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 GPUs. For each pool, the per-chain multiple sequence alignments were combined into a single AlphaFold3 input JSON (dialect alphafold3, version 1), populating unpairedMsa from the ColabFold output; pairedMsa was left empty, deferring to AlphaFold3’s internal pairing logic. AlphaFold3 was invoked via run_alphafold.py with --flash_attention_implementation=triton and --resolve_msa_overlaps=false; all other parameters retained their AlphaFold3 defaults. A single random seed (modelSeeds = [1]) was used per input, producing five diffusion-sampled structures per pool from which downstream pTM and ipTM statistics were derived as described above. In Supplementary Table 3, the resulting columns have the suffix or infix ‘_local’.

For both the local and the web-server results, the total number of predicted PPIs for each single protein is listed with the prefix ‘degree’, following notation from graph theory. Each of these columns is suffixed with 1 or 2 to indicate the monomer to which it corresponds. These degrees are calculated cumulatively at three ipTM cut-offs (see Fig. 3f): for example, ‘degree_low_webserver1’ refers to all PPIs predicted for gene 1 with low or higher confidence using the web server.

All compounds were dissolved in DMSO (VWR, V0231) and dispensed using an HP D300e digital dispenser in a 384-well plate format using a twofold dilution series. DMSO did not exceed 1% of the final culture volume and was maintained at the same concentration across all samples. Cultures were synchronized in late logarithmic phase (OD600 nm = 0.2 to 1) and then back-diluted to a starting OD600 nm of 0.01 or 0.05. Fifty microlitres of cell suspension was plated in triplicate in wells containing the test compound. Plates were incubated standing at 37 °C with 5% CO2. The OD600 nm was evaluated using a Tecan Spark or Molecular Devices SpectraMax M2 microplate reader 7–14 days after plating, and the percentage growth was calculated relative to the DMSO vehicle control for each strain. MIC90 and MIC50 measurements were calculated in R using the drm function from the drc package92, with a four-parameter log-logistic model (LL.4). For all MIC curves, data are mean ± s.e.m. for triplicates.

Compounds were dispensed in a 384-well plate as described above for the MIC assays. For each pair of drugs, all combinations of the two-dilution series were plated, including dilution series in which each drug is present alone and a DMSO control in which neither drug is present. Each combination of concentrations was plated in triplicate. Cultures were grown and plated and the relative growth was measured as described for MIC assays, except that the cultures were seeded at OD600 nm = 0.025. Drug synergy was quantified using the synergyfinder v.3.14.0 R package93. For each checkerboard, mean percentage viability values were used to calculate the Bliss independence score94,95 at each combination of drug concentrations. The resulting scores were then scanned to find the most synergistic area (MSA) and most antagonistic area (MAA). These areas were defined as the 3 × 3 contiguous areas of the plate with the highest and lowest mean Bliss scores, respectively. The mean Bliss scores of the MSA and MAA are reported for each drug combination. Both metrics are reported to avoid bias in calling a drug pair synergistic or antagonistic. Following recommended guidelines96, drug pairs with an MSA mean Bliss score higher than 15 were considered synergistic, and drug pairs with an MAA mean Bliss score lower than –15 were considered antagonistic.

A wild-type H37Rv culture was diluted to an OD600 nm of 0.05, and 500 μl of culture was added to each well of 24-well plates. Vertex-49 (6.25 μM or 12.5 μM) was added alone or in combination with either bedaquiline (0.45 μM or 0.89 μM) or ethambutol (3.61 μM or 7.21 μM) in triplicate for each concentration combination. Cultures were grown standing at 37 °C for 6 days and then plated in serial dilutions from 10−1 to 10−7 on 7H10 charcoal plates. Plates were grown for 21 days, and then colony-forming units (CFU) were counted. Because we did not have a full panel of concentration combinations, we opted to use the highest single agent (HSA) method of quantifying drug synergy97. In brief, the amount of killing (measured as the change in CFU per ml versus the no-drug control) with the combination of the two drugs is compared to the drug that shows the highest growth inhibition (the HSA) when used alone at the same concentration. The drug pair is considered synergistic if the combination of drugs results in more than 100-fold more killing than the HSA.

Cultures were grown for 5 days in 7H9-OADC with 100 ng ml−1 ATc to pre-deplete protein targets. The cultures were then washed twice in PBS containing 0.05% Tween-80 and adjusted to an OD600 nm of 0.15 with fresh 7H9-OADC. After dilution, 4-ml screw-cap glass vials were filled with the cultures, and methylene blue dye was added at a final concentration of 0.001% (w/v). All vials were sealed tightly using a PTFE–rubber seal (Thermo Fisher Scientific, C4015-21), wrapped with parafilm and incubated shaking at 60 rpm at 37 °C in an anaerobic pouch (Becton Dickinson GasPak EZ container systems, BD 260683) for 3–4 days, after which photos were taken to determine whether the cultures turned clear (intact respiration) or remained blue (impaired respiration).

A 20-ml preculture of Msm in Middlebrook 7H9 medium (Sigma) supplemented with 0.5% (w/v) bovine serum albumin, 0.08% (w/v) NaCl, 0.2% (w/v) d-glucose and 0.05% (v/v) Tween-80 was grown at 30 °C with shaking at 180 rpm to saturation. Msm with pKM444 but no other genetic modification was grown without antibiotic in the preculture medium, whereas Msm modified with a 3×Flag tag encoded in its gDNA was grown with 50 µg ml−1 hygromycin in the preculture medium. Each preculture was used to inoculate 6 l of Middlebrook 7H9 supplemented with 0.08% (w/v) NaCl, 0.2% (w/v) d-glucose, 1% (w/v) tryptone and 0.05% (v/v) Tween-80, and was grown at 30 °C with shaking at 180 rpm for 48–72 h. The cells were collected by centrifugation at 6,500g for 20 min, and pellets were resuspended in 100 ml of 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgSO4, 5 mM benzamidine HCl, 5 mM aminocaproic acid and 1 mM PMSF. The cells were lysed with the Avestin EmulsiFlex-C3 homogenizer at 20–25 kpsi, and the lysate was clarified by centrifugation at 39,000g for 30 min, followed by isolation of the membranes by centrifugation at 200,000g for 1 h. The membranes were resuspended in TBS (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl) and solubilized for 1 h with 1% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside. Solubilized membranes were centrifuged at 200,000g for 1 h to remove insoluble material before binding to around 1 ml anti-Flag M2 Affinity Gel (Sigma) in a plastic column. The column was washed with ten column volumes of TBS containing 0.05% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside before eluting the bound protein with three column volumes of 150 µg ml−1 3×Flag peptide in TBS containing 0.05% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside, followed by one column volume of TBS containing 0.05% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside. The eluted protein was concentrated with a centrifugal concentrator with 10-kDa molecular weight cut-off.

Protein (10 µg) was reduced with 20 mM dithiothreitol for 10 min at 95 °C and alkylated with 40 mM iodoacetamide for 30 min in the dark. Samples were diluted to a final concentration of 5% (w/v) SDS, and phosphoric acid was added to a final concentration of 1.2% (v/v). S-Trap protein binding buffer (165 µl) containing 90% (v/v) methanol and 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) was added to 27.5 µl acidified sample. The resulting mixture was passed through an S-trap micro column at 4,000g. The micro column was washed four times with the S-Trap protein binding buffer. Each sample was digested with 4 µg of trypsin in 20 µl of 50 mM TEAB for 1 h at 47 °C. Before elution, 4 µl of 50 mM TEAB pH 8 was added to the column. Peptides were eluted by centrifugation at 4,000g. Peptides were eluted from the column two more times with 40 µl of 0.2% (v/v) formic acid and 40 µl of 50% (v/v) acetonitrile with 0.2% (v/v) formic acid. Eluted peptides were dried and stored at –40 °C before mass-spectrometry analysis at the Network Biology Collaborative Centre at the Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute using standard protocols for data-dependent acquisition.

The SAINTexpress98,99 software package was used to score protein interactions. In brief, peptide-level counts are summed for all detected proteins for both the tagged and the untagged samples (two replicates per condition). These were then used to obtain the protein-level L2FC of counts in the tagged samples relative to the untagged samples. The SAINTexpress package uses a Bayesian model to calculate the probability of an interaction for each protein and uses these probabilities to estimate the FDR.

IMV acidification assays were performed as previously described51. In brief, the membrane fraction from wild-type, ∆qcrB and ∆ms2764 Msm strains were isolated and resuspended in IMV resuspension buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgSO4, 5 mM 6-aminocaproic acid, 5 mM benzamidine hydrochloride and 20% [v/v] glycerol). IMV acidification experiments were performed in 96-well plates (BRANDplates pureGrade 96-well black microplates). NADH and succinate were prepared as electron donors as follows. NADH was prepared immediately before use by dissolving disodium NADH in water to a final concentration of 4 mM. Succinate was prepared by dissolving sodium succinate in water to a final concentration of 20 mM. A master solution containing ACMA assay buffer (10 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl and 5 mM MgCl2), 9-amino-6-chloro-2-methoxyacridine (ACMA) dye (3.125 µM), IMVs (5 mg ml−1 total protein concentration for succinate-driven acidification; 2 mg ml−1 total protein concentration for NADH-driven acidification) and 10 µM of Q203 (with a final concentration of 2% [v/v] DMSO) or an equivalent volume of compound-free DMSO vehicle was prepared and transferred into each well of the 96-well plate. The plate was incubated in the dark for approximately 15 min at room temperature before the start of the experiment. ACMA fluorescence was measured at 25 °C with a BioTek Synergy Neo2 Hybrid Multimode plate reader (Agilent Technologies), using an excitation wavelength of 410 nm and an emission wavelength of 480 nm. IMV acidification was initiated by the addition of NADH or succinate. Fluorescence was monitored for 20 min before the addition of nigericin in ethanol to a final concentration of 2 µM with 0.02% (v/v) ethanol. Fluorescence recovery was monitored for an additional 10 min. Fluorescence recovery was calculated as the absolute difference between the fluorescence immediately before and 10 min after nigericin addition. All IMV acidification experiments were performed with at least three replicates.

Sensor spot assays were performed as described previously100.

Cultures were grown and passaged twice to closely match optical densities. Final cultures were diluted to an OD600 nm of 0.17 (around 50,000 cells per μl), and tenfold serial dilutions were made. Multichannel pipettes were used to spot 2 μl of culture for each dilution onto 7H10 with or without ATc, with the appropriate selection of antibiotics. Images were taken after approximately 20 generations.

Raw sequencing data have ben deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under project numbers PRJNA1337647, PRJNA1338999 and PRJNA1346122. Pooled AlphaFold3 co-folding used the Mtb H37Rv reference proteome (UniProt: UP000001584) and translated sequences from the Msm mc2155 reference genome (RefSeq: NC_008596.1), unless noted otherwise in the Methods. Mass-spectrometry analysis used the Msm mc2155 reference proteome (UniProt: UP000000757). sgRNA sequences were designed using the Mtb H37Rv and Msm mc2155 reference genomes (RefSeq: NC_018143.2 and RefSeq: NC_008596.1, respectively).

a, Construction of dual-sgRNA libraries. Single-sgRNA constructs were cloned individually. To assemble the dual-sgRNA library, all single-sgRNA plasmids were pooled and subjected to two parallel digestions: (1) MfeI + XhoI to generate a backbone library, and (2) EcoRI + SalI to excise the sgRNA–barcode fragment and generate an insert library. Ligation of these two products places two sgRNA cassettes in tandem, followed by their corresponding unique barcodes. To quantify sgRNA abundance, the barcode region is amplified using flanking NGS primers. b, Overview of the pilot GI library design. Up to 24 sgRNAs were selected for each of 16 target genes. The resulting dual-sgRNA library was transformed into Msm and serially passaged +/–ATc, with samples collected every 2.5 to 5 generations. The relative abundance of each sgRNA pair was quantified by sequencing the barcode region. c, Density plot of ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC projected at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs in the pilot library. Vertical lines mark the expected L2FC window between –10 and –2. d, Heat map of GI scores for all dual-targeting constructs in the pilot library. Each row and column corresponds to a single sgRNA, and each cell represents a dual-targeting construct. sgRNAs are grouped by target gene and, within each gene, are ordered by sgRNA strength, as defined by the L2FC of the sgRNA when paired with a non-targeting sgRNA at 25 generations (weaker sgRNAs at the top/left; stronger sgRNAs at the bottom/right). Gene pairs highlighted in e–h are marked with dashed boxes. e–h, Scatter plots of ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC projected at generation 25 for all dual-sgRNA constructs targeting glgB and glgE (e), ponA1 and ponA2 (f), folA and folP1 (g) and rpoB and macE (h). Vertical lines mark the expected L2FC window between –10 and –2.

a, Library metrics. Metrics are shown for the plasmid library after cloning in E. coli and for the corresponding mycobacterial library after transformation into either Msm or Mtb. Mycobacterial libraries were sequenced from the initial (Generation 0, G0) sample of the uninduced (–ATc) condition. Mtb experiment 1 and experiment 2 were derived from the same plasmid library. b,c,g,h,l,m, Heat maps of the Pearson correlation between sgRNA counts across all time points and replicates for the (b,c) Msm, (g,h) Mtb experiment 1 and (l,m) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. For each experiment, the (b,g,l) –ATc samples and (c,h,m) +ATc samples are shown on separate heat maps. d,i,n, Density plots of uncorrected ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC at 25 generations for all dual-targeting constructs in the (d) Msm, (i) Mtb experiment 1 and (n) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. e,j,o, Density plots of corrected ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC at 25 generations for all dual-targeting constructs in the (e) Msm, (j) Mtb experiment 1 and (o) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. Corrected ΔL2FC values are calculated as the residual (observed – GAM-predicted L2FC) for each dual-targeting construct. For more information, see Methods: ‘Quantification of GIs’ and Figs. 1f and 2c and Extended Data Fig. 4c. f,k,p, Density plots of GI score versus combined gene vulnerability for all gene pairs in the (f) Msm, (k) Mtb experiment 1 and (p) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. Combined gene vulnerability is defined as the sum of the vulnerabilities of the two genes in each pair.

a–l, GI scores in Mtb experiment 1 (a–f) and Mtb experiment 2 (g–l) for all genes paired with whiB7 (a,g), with ftsR (b,h), with mtrA (c,i), with ndh (d,j), with ponA1 (e,k) or with dnaE1 (f,l). Arrows mark specific interactions.

a, Distribution of observed L2FC at generation 20 for dual-NT, single-targeting, and dual-targeting constructs, as in Fig. 1b. b, Correlation of observed L2FC at generation 20 for single-targeting constructs differing only in sgRNA position. c, Expected versus observed L2FC at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs. Black line, x = y; red line, GAM fit. GI scores were computed as the median GAM residual per gene pair. d, Distribution of GI scores across all gene pairs. Shaded regions denote statistically significant (p > 0.5) interactions. e, Heat map of GI scores for all gene pairs, hierarchically clustered by Pearson correlation of GI profiles. Values beyond ±5 are clipped. f, Distribution of pairwise GI profile correlations among all sgRNAs, and among sgRNAs targeting the same gene. g, Number of positive and negative GIs (p > 0.5) per gene. h, GI scores for all genes paired with secA1 (left) or with secF (right). i, GI scores for all genes paired with murA (left) or with cwlM (right). j, Dendrogram of all genes (left), clustered by GI profile correlation. Branches are coloured by nodes enriched (FDR < 0.005) for GO terms by Fisher’s exact test. Representative clusters (right, from top to bottom: fatty acid biosynthesis, arginine biosynthesis, DNA replication, folate metabolism, thiamine metabolism, menaquinone biosynthesis, and protein degradation). k, Scatter plot comparing GI scores in Mtb experiment 1 and Mtb experiment 2, coloured by joint model hit class. See Methods for additional details. l, Distribution of GI scores for gene pairs grouped into 10 equal-width bins by GI profile correlation. Gene pairs separated by five or fewer genes were excluded to minimize potential polar effects. Boxes indicate the interquartile range (IQR), centre lines indicate the median, and whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR; outliers are not shown.

a–c, GI scores in the Msm GI screen (left) and the Mtb GI screen (right) for all genes paired with crp (a), with fumC (b) or with whiA (c). d,e, Density plots of GI scores in Msm versus Mtb for (d) all homologous gene pairs and (e) homologous gene pairs sharing the same biological process annotation (“category” in Supplementary Table 4, excluding “Unknown”). The total number of gene pairs included in each analysis (n) is indicated in the plot titles. f, Percent of Mtb GIs conserved in Msm. The two gene pair sets defined in d,e were first filtered to retain only Mtb GIs (p > 0.5 in experiment 2). An Mtb GI was considered conserved if the corresponding gene pair in Msm was also called as a significant interaction (p > 0.5) with the same sign (positive or negative). For each set, percent conservation was calculated as the number of conserved GIs divided by the number of Mtb GIs. The analysis was performed twice: once without additional filters (corresponding to the full bar height) and once excluding potential polar effects (gene pairs ≤ 5 genes apart; corresponding to the filled portion). g, Heat map of log2 odds ratio (OR), testing for enrichment or depletion of significant negative GIs (p > 0.5) within pathway pairs in Mtb, as in Fig. 3c. Only results with q < 0.05 are shown. Hollow circles indicate pathway pairs that fail this threshold after removing possible polar effects (gene pairs ≤ 5 genes apart).

a, Co-folding pool sizes (number of monomers) generated by size-aware bin packing for all gene pairs screened in Msm. All pools have exactly one copy of each monomer (that is, the co-folding screen captures only heterodimers). Six additional pools with >25 monomers not shown. b, Co-folding pool sizes (total residues) generated by size-aware bin packing for all gene pairs screened in Msm. 40 additional pools with fewer than 4,450 residues not shown. c, Co-folding pool sizes (number of monomers) for all gene pairs screened in Mtb, as in a. Five pools with >25 monomers not shown. d, Co-folding pool sizes (total residues) for all gene pairs screened in Mtb, as in b. 36 pools with fewer than 4,450 residues not shown. e, Uncorrected mean ipTM scores for all gene pairs screened in Mtb. Red line is the correction factor, calculated as (0.0044 × \(\sqrt{{l}_{1}\,+\,{l}_{2}}\,\)) − 0.036, where (l1, l2) are the lengths of each protein in the pair. f, Size-corrected (s.c.) mean ipTM scores for all gene pairs screened in Mtb. g,h, Distribution of s.c. ipTMs for co-folded Msm protein pairs with mean s.c. ipTM ≥ 0.2 (g) and all protein pairs (h). Black dots and grey lines represent the mean and s.d. of s.c. ipTMs across all pools.

a, Volcano plot showing results from an Mtb CRISPRi-based CGI screen with the KasA and KasB inhibitor thiolactomycin. Knockdown of kasA and pptT sensitizes Mtb to thiolactomycin, whereas knockdown of rpoB does not. FDR was calculated using α-RRA with one-sided tests for enrichment and depletion. b–k, Checkerboard assay heat maps showing Bliss scores for the indicated drug pairs in Mtb, as in Fig. 4g,i,j,l. b, Known synergistic pair: RpoB inhibitor rifampicin (RIF) and EmbA and EmbB inhibitor ethambutol (EMB); c, Known additive pair: ribosome inhibitor linezolid (LZD) and EMB; d, Thiolactomycin (TLM) and LZD; e, TLM and EMB; f, PptT inhibitor 8918 and LZD; g, 8918 and EMB; h, Pks13 inhibitor mCMX410 and LZD; i, EfpA inhibitor BRD-8000.3 and LZD; j, PknA and PknB inhibitor Vertex-49 (V49) and EMB; and k, V49 and ATP synthase inhibitor bedaquiline (BDQ). n = 3 biological replicates.

a–e, GI scores for all genes paired with rpoB (a), with atpB (b), with nadA (c), with nadB (d) or with nadD (e). Arrows mark specific interactions.

a–g, Each panel corresponds to a distinct gene: (a) clpX, (b) inhA, (c) dprE1, (d) mmpL3, (e) pks13, (f) glcB, and (g) fusA1. Histograms show the distribution of GI scores for all genes paired with the gene indicated in the plot title. Adjacent plots show dose–response curves (mean ± s.e.m., n = 3 biological replicates) for hypomorphic CRISPRi knockdown (KD) strain(s) and a non-targeting (NT) control strain in the presence of the drug indicated on the x axis. ATc was added five days prior to the assay. Knockdown–drug pairings were selected to test whether negative GIs predict drug sensitization, by combining genetic inhibition of one gene with pharmacological inhibition of its interaction partner. Control drug–KD pairings not predicted to induce sensitization based on GI data are shown on the left and test drug(s) are shown to the right. Drugs include: DnaN inhibitor griselimycin (GRIS); InhA inhibitors isoniazid (INH) and NITD-916; DprE1 inhibitors PBTZ169 and BTZ043; MmpL3 inhibitors AU1235 and SQ109; Pks13 inhibitor mCMX410; GlcB inhibitor JSF1305; FusA1 inhibitor fusidic acid (FUS); and control antibiotics clarithromycin (CLR; 50S ribosome) and streptomycin (STR; 30S ribosome).

a, A representative cluster from the GI profile dendrogram in Mtb reveals a coherent module of ETC-associated genes along with several genes of unknown function. #1615. Michael Carrick future: Review 'ongoing' at Man United - what will be the outcome?

By Matt Law | 09 Nov 2026 18:27

Manchester United's director of football Jason Wilcox is reportedly leading the review into Michael Carrick's future at Old Trafford.

A disastrous start to the 2026-27 campaign has left Man United down in 18th spot in the Premier League table, with the team winning just one of their first 10 league games of the season.

Man United did manage to beat Roma 3-2 in the Champions League last week, though, before twice coming from two goals behind to draw 4-4 with Aston Villa in the Premier League on Sunday, and the season has now been interrupted by an international break.

There is huge uncertainty when it comes to Carrick's future, with the sporting department at Old Trafford now reviewing the head coach's position.

According to The Guardian, Wilcox is leading the review, with chief executive Omar Berrada also being consulted, before a recommendation is made to Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

Carrick was expected to be sacked by Man United off the back of the 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth on October 25, but he was allegedly given three games to save his job - the trip to Chelsea in the Premier League, followed by the games against Roma and Villa.

It is understood that Eddie Howe is Wilcox's number one choice to replace Carrick, should a change be made, but that is not thought to be a view universally shared by the decision-makers.

Man United are next in action at Anfield on November 22, facing Liverpool in the Premier League, before facing Sporting Lisbon away from home in the Champions League.

November will then conclude with a home league game against Brentford.

"We’re in November. I don’t like the situation we’re in or the results we’ve had, but we can definitely do something about it. We haven’t won enough games but I expect to move forward," Carrick told Sky Sports News after the draw with Villa.

"We’ll keep working on the things we’ve been working on, and tighten up on a few mistakes and win football matches."

The positions of both Wilcox and Berrada have also been called into question due to Man United's ongoing struggles, and the pair are facing uncertain futures.

There remain calls from the club's supporters for the Glazer family to sell their share of the 20-time English champions, but there are no indications at this stage that will occur.

As it stands, Carrick is likely to remain in charge of Man United for the Liverpool game, with the Englishman still being backed despite the team's struggles this season.

#1613. Mum rushes to goalkeeper in Spanish football's killer collision: Jesus Owono suffering 'hardest days of his life' and being comforted after striker he clashed with died from 'chest trauma'

Published: 05:24 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 05:29 EST, 6 November 2026

Goalkeeper Jesus Owono's doting mum has rushed to Andorra to comfort him as he endures the 'hardest days of his life' following his death clash with a rival striker whose funeral took place yesterday.

Maria del Carmen Owono Mangue made the five-and-a-half-hour drive from her home in the Basque city of San Sebastian to Andorra where her 25-year-old son currently plays his football after learning Jesus de Miguel had lost his fight for life in a Tenerife hospital.

She and the Andorra FC keeper have been deeply close since he moved to San Sebastian from their native Equatorial Guinea as an eight-year-old boy to rejoin her after she had emigrated earlier in search of work to provide for her family and an aunt had taken the youngster into her home.

Owono, the eldest of six siblings, has admitted of his arrival in a new country: 'I came in pursuit of a dream, not the dream of playing football, but the dream of being with my mother.'

His mum has confessed: 'Waking up in the morning and seeing your child doing what they love most is a mother's greatest joy.'

She said in the same interview when the goalkeeper was just 20 in comments which could now come back to haunt the family: 'He needs to keep working. We still don't know what will happen. If God allows things to turn out well for him and if not, well, you know that he has worked hard and done what he could.'

Goalkeeper Jesus Owono is suffering and being comforted after his killer collision

Owono, who has closed his social media accounts, has had his mother rush to his side in the days following Jesus de Miguel's death (Source: Instagram)

Overnight one of Jesus' younger brothers confirmed their mum was by his side in Andorra.

Speaking from the second-floor four-bed apartment she owns in a tree-lined street in a middle-class residential neighbourhood east of San Sebastian's city centre, he said: 'We're all very distraught. My mum has gone to be with Jesus because he is suffering.'

A source close to the goalkeeper added: 'Maria del Carmen is one of the most important, if not the most important, people in Jesus' life.

'He had a difficult start being separated from his mum at such an early age and it was very difficult for her too.

'They have been inseparable since Jesus moved to Spain as an eight-year-old.

'Maria del Carmen has helped him integrate into completely new surroundings and supported him every step of the way on his road to becoming a professional footballer.

De Miguel and Owono collided - and hours later the former died of 'accidental chest trauma'

De Miguel's team-mates are pictured arriving at his funeral in Navahermosa on Thursday

'It's only natural that she'd want to be by his side now when by his own admission he's in pieces and finding it impossible to come to terms with the fact a fellow footballer has died because of something he did.'

From the FC Andorra supporters' section, we want to send you all our support and love during these tough and difficult times.

We are aware of the suffering you are going through after what happened. We know these aren't easy days, but we want you to remember one thing: you are not alone.

You have your family, your friends, your team-mates, the staff, and the entire club by your side. But you also have us, a fanbase that appreciates you, respects you, and today, more than ever, wants to send you all our love and support.

We also want you to know that we categorically reject all the insults, threats, and judgments you've been receiving lately. An accident doesn't define a person, much less their character.

We don't want the pain, anger, or helplessness to turn into hatred towards you. Behind the footballer is a person, with feelings and a family who are also suffering.

We want you to know that this is your home. When you return to the pitch, to defend our goal and wear this jersey again, you'll have a stand that will still be by your side, cheering you on as always.

Now you don't have to prove anything to anyone. It won't be easy and it will take time, but even though it's difficult and painful, we have to move forward, we have to work to recover that fighting spirit and smile that are so characteristic of you. The most important thing now is your recovery, but along the way, know that you can count on us, that you're not alone.

Stay strong, Jesus. We're with you. Our Spider Man today, tomorrow, and always.

Some of Owono's Andorra FC team-mates and members of the club's supporters' group have also paid him a visit to deliver a letter of encouragement.

The letter refers to the goalkeeper as 'their Spiderman,' 'his joy,' and 'a person with feelings and a strong family connection.'

Owono was red-carded after kneeing the 30-year-old CD Tenerife striker in the chest in a reckless tackle late into stoppage time during a second-division match on Monday.

The match was suspended when the two sides were drawing 2-2.

Tragic Jesus, whose partner Marta Fernandez and one-year-old daughter Carla were watching from the stands, was reportedly revived by paramedics on the pitch after going into cardiac arrest before being rushed to hospital.

His club confirmed around 9.30am local time on Tuesday he had died about 8am the same day, saying they were 'heartbroken' and had a 'lump in their throats' after revealing earlier the footballer's neurological condition had worsened.

A post-mortem concluded in a preliminary report his death was consistent with 'accidental chest trauma' although the results of further tests conducted during the autopsy are still pending.

Owono used 'excessive force' while contesting the ball near the half-way line according to the match referee's report.

He is facing a lengthy ban and possible criminal charges after police in Tenerife confirmed homicide squad officers were looking into whether had committed an involuntary manslaughter.

Legal experts have cast doubt on the possibility of prosecution because the clash that resulted in Jesus de Miguel's death occurred during open play.

The first photos of the dead footballer's partner emerged overnight as his team-mates prepared to travel to the small town of Navahermosa, 80 miles south-west of Madrid, where his devastated parents come from.

Jesus' mum and dad made the return trip after jetting to Tenerife to try to reach their son before he died in hospital on Tuesday morning hours after his clash with Owono.

The father was watching the match in a bar in his home town when he saw him slump to the ground.

Equatorial Guinea international Owono, who turned round as he headed back to the dressing rooms following his sending off and walked back to the player he had hurt after realising how seriously injured the Tenerife frontman was, broke his silence on Wednesday.

The father of De Miguel, is hugged at his son's wake, three days on from his death

The football world has rallied behind De Miguel and his family with tributes to the striker

A neighbour said De Miguel's father (pictured right, with his mother, girlfriend and sister R-L) burst into tears after seeing the impact of the collision on television. (Source: Instagram/martitamig)

He released a statement via his club that said: 'These are the most difficult days of my life.

'I am struggling to find the words, and it is very hard for me to process anything that has happened.

'I feel immense pain over the loss of Jesus. I am thinking of him, his family, and all the people who loved him.

'I know there will be many matters to address, and I will face whatever comes with complete respect.

'But right now, honestly, I cannot think of anything other than Jesus and the grief we are experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesus.'

FC Andorra, reacting to news of the Tenerife striker's death in hospital, said on Tuesday morning: 'Heartbroken and devastated, we wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife.

#1611. Man Utd impress in draw against PSG but injury worries mount

Michael Carrick said he had to be careful with Mason Mount after the England midfielder handed Manchester United an injury scare in their friendly draw with Paris St Germain.

Mount has had a torrid time with injuries since signing from Chelsea in a £55m-deal three years ago, starting only 25 Premier League games for United in that time.

The 27-year-old has been successfully deployed by Carrick in a central midfield role during pre-season, leading to speculation that United may not make another expected signing in that department.

But Mount played only 18 minutes of Saturday’s 1-1 draw against the European champions in Gothenburg before being replaced by Scotland international Tyler Fletcher.

“He [Mount] got kicked. We just wanted to be careful and look after him,” Carrick, the United head coach, told reporters in Sweden.

“We’ve been lucky with injuries so far, so we wanted to be careful.”

Post-match video footage showed Mount walking freely on to the United bus without the aid of a protective boot or knee support.

Michael Carrick told VG Mason Mount was taken off as a precaution. Looked OK leaving stadium. pic.twitter.com/Uo0fBtgpAl

United went behind within two minutes at the Ullevi Stadium when Liverpool target Ibrahim Mbaye punished slack marking to put PSG ahead.

Bryan Mbeumo fired United level after 32 minutes following good work from Amad Diallo, the Cameroon forward’s third goal in two games after his match-winning double against Atletico Madrid.

United meet Leeds in a Dublin friendly on Wednesday before coming up against AC Milan and their former manager Ruben Amorim next Saturday.

United open their Premier League campaign at Hull on August 22.

“It was good game. PSG is good so we had to keep building fitness. I am happy to have other [players] back and we have to keep going.”

“It’s good for me. I enjoyed it. We need to build fitness, we have a big season ahead.”

“It’s a good game PSG are tough to beat and we got a draw and now think about the next game [against Leeds in Dublin].”

“We have two more games against Leeds a and Milan. We need to have big season and hope to win a trophy.”

All over in Gothenburg and it’s been a good match for Michael Carrick’s team. They looked sharper and quicker than their win over Atletico Madrid last week (what the manager wanted) and things are moving in the right direction. Two things to worry about, however, were the early exits of Mason Mount and Tom Heaton with injuries. They’ll especially hope the Mount knock isn’t anything mid or long term.

Nearly done and it’s been a good run out for United. They’ve looked the better, sharper side and, if anything, deserve to win. In mitigation, this is United fourth pre-season game to PSG’s second...

Fernandes has one thing on his mind when he gets the ball 25 yards out in the centre of the park - a shot. He unleashes the attempt, destined for the bottom-left corner, forcing Longoni, the sub goalkeeper, into a good save.

Two chances for United in quick succession. A lovely ball from the middle of the park by Zirkzee finds Dalot on the right. He chips the ball to the back post where one of the Fletchers (sorry, I am not sure which) heads for goal. His attempt is blocked and the ball, ultimately, falls at the feet of Lacey whose shot is blazed high over the bar.

There have been plenty of good things for Carrick to take from this match. The passing, while not of the standard of a cut-and-thrust Premier League match, has been good for the time of year, and there have been enough flashes of brilliance/class/invention etc to suggest that pre-season is moving in the right direction.

Lovely bit of play by United. A great pass with the outside of the boot from the inside-left channel by Tielemans finds Fernandes who plays a sidefooted shot that goes just wide.

Tielemans’s first bit of brilliance from the Belgian there.

Both sides losing possession a fair bit at the moment. Strong pre-season vibes right now.

Maguire has had a good game. He’s played a number of long passes from the back and looked assured. This time he’s up in the PSG half and decides to have a pop - his shot testing Safanov, who saves well.

Had there been VAR Safanov might have had something to answer for...he may have beaten Zirkzee to the ball but he flew in the air and jurt the United man in the process.

Anwway, there’s no VAR (hurrah, for those of you who consider it a modern-day evil) and it doesn’t matter.

Chance for United to go ahead and it comes from two things. (i) A long, hopeful ball from Fernandes that looks for Zirkzee (ii) Safanov rushing off his line and into no-man’s land. The ball comes loose and Jack Fletcher, instead of having a go at goal, with the keeper on the ground and out of the game, passes to Lacey whose shot is wide.

Tyler Fletcher loses the ball near the United half and it, ultimately, results in a PSG corner. From the set piece United defend well and snuff out all hint of danger.

PSG seeing more of the ball at the moment. They work the ball to the right and Amass brings down Mbaye.

From the resulting free-kick, in the final third, the French side whip in the ball but Mee is up ot the challenge and come to collect well.

Santos, Mbeumo, Shaw, Amad, Lacey are off

Fernandes, Jack Feltcher, Zirkzee and Amass are on.

A raft of changes for PSG sees Marquinhos and João Neves, among others, come on. More like it, in terms of first-team ‘names’, on the pitch for the European Cup champions.

United on top in this half, as they were in the first.

The paces quickens and the game is much better for it. Mbuemo drives toward the PSG box, he cuts inside from the right before unleashing a shot that is bound for the back of the net before a fine one-handed save by Safanov. Credit, too, for Maguire whose long ball from the back found Mbuemo brilliantly. Promising...

Lacey tries to play in Dorgu on the left but he’s asking too much of his team-mate. Wonder when the expected raft of changes will take place?

Slow start to the second half. This is very much pre-season-friendly pace.

Having seen Mount limp off in the first half, there’s more worry at the start of the second and Heaton is force off with what looks like a hamstrung injury. He dashed off his line to clear a ball and in doing so has tweaked something. Mee replaces him.

Back under way Gothenburg - there have been a number of changes and will bring them to you once I’ve worked out who has come on and who they’ve replaced.

A world record that still stands...(this was back in 1995).

And that is it for the first 45 minutes. PSG took the early lead, but from that moment on United have been the better side and deservedly are level through Mbueno’s goal.

There will be one minute of added time at the end of what has been a good first half for Man Utd.

Amad has a go from outside the box forcing the save from Safanov. He’s such a live wire and one of the best in his position in the top flight. Him or Antony? No contest, strange it took United a while to work that one out.

Yet more good work from the underrated Amad. He again closes down well on the right before winning back possession and cutting the ball back for Lacey. To think he was starring for Sunderland in the Championship while Antony was starting for United...

United have been the better side since conceding earlier and, as if to illustrate my point, as I typed that an Mbuemo free-kick is well saved by Safanov. That was heading for the top-right bin.

Great work on the left by Dorgu and Shaw ends with the latter chipping the ball to the back post where Amad is lurking with intent. The Ivorian looks to head the ball home, but before he can get anything on it it looks as though he’s pushed in the back. United players are sure it’s a penalty but, more importantly, the referee doesn’t.

Amad does brilliantly, winning the ball off Koukaba in the final third, from there he scampers toward the box before playing in Mbuemo who takes one touch before firing in a shot into the bottom right corner of the net.

Free-kick for PSG on the right, near the final third. The ball comes in and it’s straight into the arms of Heaton in the United goal.

Kvaratskhelia, not seen much of him so far, runs into the box, but Amad does well to usher him back out.

The match is pedestrian at the moment, but as I type that, Dorgu, yep, him again, drives down the left and puts in a good cross that is well intercepted by Safanov in the PSG goal.

United continue to see more of the ball, Dorgu’s seeing more of it than most. But, no chances really fashioned, still, plenty of time to go.

Worry for United having to sub off Mount. It looks as though he took a knock to a foot and Carrick and co will hope it’s not a long-term injury. Mount, who’s had a good pre-season, has been replaced by Fletcher, son of Darren.

Foul on Mazraoui results in two things. The Mount has to come off, and, United have a free-kick on the edge of the PSG area.

From the set-piece Mbuemo has a go and it’s a regulation save from Safonov in the PSG goal.

Heaven loses possession in the middle of the park and from there it’s like the parting of the Red Sea as PSG have a three-on-one. Mbaye gets the shot in on goal but Andrey Santos covers back brilliantly and does enough to get something on the ball. He’s started both this match and pre-season well.

United are looking half decent on the ball. They’re passing it well and not afraid to switch things around.

A lovely long ball from Maguire finds Dorgo whose lovely first touch takes him into the box before a cut back is intercepted by a PSG man. Promising signs though for Carrick’s men.

United seeing more of the ball at the moment. They’re being patient but cannot fashion an opening and the ball is worked all the way back to Heaton in goal.

Needless to say this is being played at a slowish pace...no blood-and-guts challenges being put in.

Good work down the right sees Amad plays in Shay Lacey who crosses into the box. The ball find shte head of Mbuemo and the ball sails over the bar. Better from United.

United started slowly against Atletico and they’ve done the same here.

Bright start to say the least from the French side. They work the ball left and it’s an easy cross from Dro Fernandez for Mbaye to tap home for the very early lead.

They’re under way in Sweden. United are in their new vibrant red kit and PSG in their blue, red and white kit. Big fan of the French side’s kit, it harks back to the kit they had in the 1990s when the likes of George Weah and David Ginola were entertaining in the capital of France.

Man Utd: Heaton, Mazraoui, Maguire, Heaven, Shaw, Mount, Santos, Dorgu, Lacey, Amad, Mbeumo; Subs: Heath, Mee, Amass, Armer, Dalot, Yoro, Fernandes, J. Fletcher, T. Fletcher, Tielemans, Zirkzee

Paris St-Germain: Safonov, Pacho, Zabarnyi, Koukaba, Boly, Beraldo, Dro, Mayulu, Kvaratskhelia, Ayari, Mbaye; Subs: Marquinhos, Mendes, Lucea, Vitinha, Neves, El Nay, Idder, Drame, Bourdin, Ndjantou, Meite, Longoni, Chevalier

And here’s a famous match that took place there, giving a certain Sir Alex Ferguson his first European trophy.

“Get a bit sharper, get better on the ball, go up a notch.”

“It’s not about today it’s about preparing. Some players have played 90 minutes, some have played three games, some have just come back. So it’s about keeping working on things we’ve been working on.”

“They’re similar to us, but have fewer senior players available . They’ve had a great time and great squad so whoever on the pitch it will be a test.”

A hugely talented player for a number of clubs, including United, who ever really lived up to his early promise.

Good to have you back, lads 🇵🇹 pic.twitter.com/3EgkXLqcQm

📃 Le onze de départ pour cette rencontre de préparation face à Manchester United. #PSGMUN pic.twitter.com/LodcDM1Yrm

I expect they’ll make an appearence at some point.

Ready to face PSG in our latest pre-season test ✊

Manchester United continue their Sweden sojourn with match against Paris St-Germain in Gothenburg.

Clearly a clash against the back-to-back Champions League winners is a step up from their previous two pre-season friendlies (victories against Rosenborg and Atletico Madrid), but at the same time this is more a chance for players to get miles in the legs and see how new signings and possibly some young guns fit in.

One of those new signings is Youri Tielemans, and the Belgian international is in line to make his debut after his move from Aston Villa. Other team news is that Bruno Fernandes is back and ready to captain the team.

Michael Carrick has also been boosted by the returns of Matheus Cunha, Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui after their post-World Cup breaks.

Cunha, however, will not play a part in today’s match because of a “minor illness” according to the MUTV website. He is expected to link up with the squad in Ireland, where they face Leeds United at Croke Park, after the match.

This will be Man Utd’s first outing since the 2-1 win over Atletico, a performance and result that pleased Carrick.

“I enjoyed it, I thought there was a lot of good in things that we are looking to improve on,” the United manager said. “Building on what we did for the last seven months, I think there is a lot of good signs for us, it’s never going to be the exact stage we want to be at. But I thought there was really a lot of positives to take out of the game, individual, collectively as a team, senior players looking strong and fit, and the younger players doing really well.

“The spirit and the camaraderie is so important for the team, it’s great to see the boys getting on so naturally and enjoying each other’s company. Collectively we looked strong as a team, which is always the most important thing, and individual performances seeing the young players come on to have an impact.”

#1610. Man United players causing themselves "emotional damage" amid ongoing struggles

By Matt Law | 09 Nov 2026 19:01

Former Manchester United captain Gary Neville has said that the club's players are almost causing themselves "emotional damage" with their post-match walks of honour.

The Red Devils are currently down in 18th spot in the Premier League table and have incredibly won just one of their opening 10 matches of their league campaign.

Following 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth at the end of October, Man United's players were booed off the field, shortly after the supporters had sung the name of head coach Michael Carrick.

The players were given a much warmer sent-off following Sunday's 4-4 draw with Aston Villa in the Premier League, but captain Bruno Fernandes in particular had a pained expression on his face when he clapped all four sides of the stadium.

Neville has said that the walks of honour are becoming "painful to watch" and claimed that the players are almost causing themselves "emotional damage".

"You have got to admire their persistence, they kept going," Neville told NBC Sports. "The defensive errors were shocking and we'll discuss that shortly. But this lap around the pitch.

"I played for Manchester United 602 times and I always appreciated the fans at the end of the game, but this pattern of them walking around the pitch after defeats by Bournemouth and a 4-4 at home against Aston Villa, it's almost painful to watch. They're almost causing themselves emotional damage.

"This just can't go on, can it? It's absolutely desperate. Michael will be proud of them and the fans are singing his name because they love him but this is a really sorry situation."

Carrick's future is currently the subject of a review, led by the club's sporting director Jason Wilcox, while chief executive Omar Berrada is also involved.

Once the review has been concluded, Wilcox and Berrada are set to make a recommendation to co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe over the route forward for the club.

Carrick has insisted that he will not be resigning as head coach, and as it stands, the Englishman will lead the team into their clash with Liverpool after the November international break.

"It's not going to happen, no," Carrick told Sky Sports News on Sunday when asked whether he could resign following the clash with Villa.

Senior figures at Man United allegedly have different views when it comes to a suitable replacement for Carrick, which is one of the main reasons why a change has not been made.

#1608. Italy squad: Five players to watch under Roberto Mancini this month including Chelsea, Como, AC Milan stars

By Oliver Thomas | 09 Nov 2026 20:30

Roberto Mancini has named his latest Italy squad ahead of two UEFA Nations League fixtures against France and Belgium during the November international break.

A place in the quarter-finals is up for grabs and the Azzurri currently sit second in League A Group 1, three points behind leaders France and only one point above Belgium in third.

Italy will welcome France to San Siro for their penultimate group fixture on Thursday, before travelling to Brussels for a potentially pivotal clash with Belgium on Sunday.

From breakout starlets making waves in Serie A and the Champions League to high-profile Premier League imports looking to cement their status, Mancini’s 32-man squad is a bold blend of elite experience and vibrant, emerging youth.

These two upcoming fixtures present the perfect stage for several Azzurri stars to stake their long-term claims in the senior side, and here, Sports Mole takes a closer look at five players to watch out for during this month’s international break.

AC Milan’s breakout starlet has taken to Serie A by storm after making a prolific start to the 2026-27 campaign, scoring eight goals in 13 appearances across all competitions.

The electrifying 20-year-old midfielder recently made history as the youngest Italian ever to score a hat-trick in a major European competition during a 4-0 Europa League win over Red Bull Salzburg.

Mancini’s decision to award Cisse his first senior call-up reflects a hunger to inject fresh, dynamic energy into the Azzurri attack.

"I have a lot of desire. I want to prove my qualities. I hope to have the chance, and being there is a source of great pride,” Cisse told reporters as he reacted to his maiden Azzurri call-up.

Cisse is certainly one to watch as he bids to translate his impressive club form and clinical tempo-changing ability onto the international stage against elite opposition.

At the age of just 19, attacking midfielder Mattia Liberali has enjoyed a lively start to life under Cesc Fabregas at Como following his €6m summer move from AC Milan.

Once compared to Phil Foden by Milan legend Alessandro Costacurta, Liberali marked his first and only Serie A start of the season with a goal in a 3-1 victory over Fiorentina last month.

The right-sided winger also made a notable impression as a second-half substitute in Como’s record-breaking 9-1 away triumph over Lens in the Champions League, scoring once and providing two assists during a 32-minute cameo.

Liberali’s exceptional technical ability, creativity and eye for a pass have prompted Mancini to fast-track him to the senior set-up, just a month after making his Under-21 debut for the Azzurri.

Having already tasted European success as a Under-17 European Championship winner with Italy, Liberali provides a fascinating creative weapon for the upcoming Nations League double-header.

“Liberali is a very good player with great quality,” Mancini told reporters on Monday. “He has made only a few Serie A appearances, but he did very well at youth level. All the young players here have impressed us and given us positive signs.”

Standing at an imposing 6ft 5in at the age of just 18, Udinese centre-back Matteo Palma has earned his first ever call-up to the senior Italy squad after Gianluca Mancini pulled out due to injury.

Born in Berlin, Palma previously represented Italy at the Under-15s level before playing for Germany's youth ranks up to the Under-18s, but he has now filed a switch back to the Azzurri.

Gifted with immense physical strength, excellent positioning and comfortable progression on the ball, Palma has stood out as a lone bright spark in a struggling Udinese side sitting rock bottom of the Serie A table, recently cementing his place with four consecutive 90-minute outings.

Palma has naturally drawn comparisons to Atalanta BC’s Giorgio Scalvini and Mancini believes that the teenager has the potential to “become a very good defender” for the national team in years to come.

Confronting heavyweights France and Belgium this month will be the ultimate test of his maturity and high tactical intelligence, should he be thrown into Mancini’s team straight away.

After being named the 2025-26 Serie A Defender of the Year on loan at Cagliari, Marco Palestra earned a high-profile £43m move from Atalanta to Chelsea this summer, but his start to life at Stamford Bridge has been disrupted by injury.

The 21-year-old was limited to just 43 minutes of action across Chelsea’s opening eight Premier League games, but he has since started the last two for Xabi Alonso’s side, including a 2-0 home win over Manchester United.

Blessed with an athletic physique and explosive pace, Palestra is comfortable operating as either a traditional full-back or a modern wing-back on either side of the defence, with his versatility being a key trait admired by Mancini.

Palestra made his senior international debut for Italy back in March and although he has only just recovered from injury, Mancini feels that the time is right to recall the youngster this month.

Not only will Palestra rival Michael Kayode for a place on the right side of defence, but he will also provide competition for both Federico Dimarco and Riccardo Calafiori on the left.

The most-capped player in Italy’s current squad is goalkeeper and captain Gianluigi Donnarumma, who is expected to earn his 88th and 89th caps against France and Belgium this month.

Despite the 27-year-old’s world-class status, recent scrutiny over a plethora of high-profile mistakes at club level with Man City has increased the pressure on the shot-stopper to deliver a flawless international break.

Donnarumma has been part of a Citizens side that has conceded 17 goals across their last eight matches in all competitions, while he has failed to keep a clean sheet with Italy in any of his four Nations League appearances.

Improvements between the sticks from Donnarumma will be essential if a transitioning Azzurri side hopes to keep France and Belgium quiet as well as advance to the quarter-finals.

However, failure to deliver two commanding performances will only intensify the debate over whether Donnarumma should be taken out of the firing line, opening the door for hungry rivals at both club and international level.
