#1607. Chelsea’s feisty friendly ends in penalty shoot-out confusion

Chelsea’s Far East tour ended in farce and confusion with players waiting around for a penalty shoot-out that never happened.

The chaos came at the end of a hard-earned, bad-tempered draw against Malaysian champions Johor Darul Ta’zim, with an own-goal in the 89th minute sparring the west London side’s blushes.

That goal also was supposed to set up penalties. But after minutes of waiting around – and Kevin Campello, Chelsea’s head of first-team operations, saying “it’s written in the contract” – the players walked off the pitch.

That confusion ended a feisty affair in which tensions threatened to boil over and that, at certain points, paid little attention to the “friendly” aspect of the clash with seven yellow cards shown. At one point the visitors’ new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee exchanged angry words with some of Johor’s coaching staff. The CFC TV commentary team suggested that the spot-kicks were abandoned because of the match’s heated atmosphere.

Austin MacPhee was ready to throw hands😂 pic.twitter.com/CFDgTOwmxE

Having played just 24 hours earlier in Jakarta – a 3-0 win over AC Milan – it was no surprise to see Xabi Alonso name a fresh XI, a mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters given much-needed game time.

And considering Johor are one game away from setting a new world record of 109 matches unbeaten in the top flight – a run that would surpass the current mark set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s – it was also no shock to see the Malaysian team offer a stern, pre-season test for the west Londoners.

After a good start Chelsea were second best in a first half in which Johor should have been at least two goals to the good. The Malaysian champions controlled the first 45 minutes and were 1-0 up after 14 minutes – a low cross from the left side-footed home by Arif Aiman.

The hosts gave the young, inexperienced Chelsea backline a torrid time, especially on the flanks and Óscar Arribas was guilty of not capitalising on a great chance to double Johor’s lead, his shot after cutting in from the right going wide.

While they looked vulnerable at the back, Chelsea also struggled to keep possession in attack. But they got an equaliser they scarcely deserved after Liam Delap was manhandled to the ground in the box by Kevin Medina. The striker, who may well leave Stamford Bridge before the transfer window slams shut, fired home the spot-kick allowing the visitors to go into the break on level terms.

For the most part, the second half followed a similar pattern to the first – Jofor having the better chances, while tensions on the pitch continued to run high.

It was, however, Chelsea who took the lead after the break, Delap once again scoring from the spot, this time after Jamie Gittens was brought down in the area.

Johor, though, kept on creating, thanks in part to a fairly porous visitors’ backline, and levelled through a deflected Arribas free kick, before going 3-2 up thanks thanks to a well-taken Bérgson strike.

Had it stayed that way Chelsea could have had few complaints. But as the clock approached 90 minutes, the visitors had one last attack. Mykhailo Mudryk, just on as a substitute, delivered a cross from the left that Antonio Glauder could only steer into his own net. That was supposed to set up the penalty shoot-out that did not take place and the chance for one of the sides to claim a hollow victory.

Considering a raft of changes and that fact this was far from the first XI, it is hard to know what to make of this. But among the positive things Alonso could take from the game was the impressive form of Nicolas Jackson and good centre-forward play of Delap. The negative was, however, a poor defensive display.

Chelsea return to Stamford Bridge on Saturday for their last pre-season friendly, against Real Sociedad, before the Premier League season starts away at local rivals Fulham on August 24.

Johor Darul Ta’zim: Syihan Hazmi; Arribas, Israfilov (Carlos Akapo 82), Medina, Antonio Glauder, Silva (La’Vere Corbin-Ong 89); Arif Aiman, Petrovic, Méndez (Nené 78), Marcos Guilherme (Bérgson); Zahedi (Stoichkov 62). Substitutes: Abad, Davies, Hidalgo, Nahuel Leiva, Lowry, Mohamadou Sumareh, Stuart Wilkin.Booked: Israfilov, Antonio Glauder, Silva.Goals: Arif Aiman (14), Arribas (65), Bérgson (86).Chelsea: Sharman-Lowe (Slolina 46); Subuloye, Adarabioyo, Anselmino (Watson 29); Geovany Quenda, Dario Essugo, Nicoll-Jazuli, Gittens (Mudryk 87); Estêvão, Delap, Jacskon (Satpaev 86). Substitutes: Curd, Diakite, Kavuma-McQueen, Sarr, Walsh.Booked: Estêvão, Delap, Jackson, Geovany Quenda, Watson.Goals: Delap (42 pen, 62 pen), Antonio Glauder (89 og).

There will NOT be a penalty shootout. No one is quite sure why.

Anyway, that was an entertaining draw, plenty of good things for Chelsea (the play of Delap and Jackson) as well as worrying signs (open and vulnerable at the back).

The commentators on CFC TV are now not so sure!

That was an entertaining pre-season friendly. There was a bit of niggle and that added to the action.

There will be penalties, apparently, if it stays the same score...

Will there be a late winner? There will be four minutes of added time.

Mudryk just on picks up the ball on the left and, with four Chelsea players in the box, crosses into the danger area. It’s a good ball and asks too many questions of the hosts as Glauder diverts the ball into his own net.

It’s what the host have, on the balance of play, deserved, but it’s a gift from Chelsea. Essugo loses the ball in the final third and Bergson, on as sub pick it put driving at the box before hitting a low shot from outside the area, the ball nestling in the left corner of the net.

Chelsea have been better this half than the first 45, they’ve been able to control the pace of the game well since the break.

The pace has slowed down since the break, Chelsea seeing more of the ball. They work it right before Watson loses possession on the edge of the area.

The referee clearly forgot about the hydration break and the two teams are having a belated one now. Delightful...

I reckon there’s another goal left in this match. It’s been entertaining fare and the hosts have given as good as they’ve got, if not more.

This has been a lively match, better than most run-of-the-mill pre-season friendlies. Chelsea seeing a fair bit of possession at the moment, can they fashion a chance?

Yes they can. But it’s a longish shot from Gittens that is easily saved by Hamzi in the JDT goal.

More niggle in this match that hasn’t really had many tough challenges. After a few handbags the referee takes control and the argy bargy peters out.

It’s the least the hosts deserve. They have a free-kick 25 yards out, Arribas takes it with his right it’s at the wall but in turning away from the ball Delap deflects it into the far-right corner giving Slonina no chance.

Fluky goal but the hosts have deserved their bit of luck.

Delap again with the goal, this time he goes low, but still to the keeper’s right.

Penalty for Chelsea. Gittens cuts back in the box onto his right and is clipped by the defender. Clear-cut penalty.

Half-chance for Delap on the edge of the area. He playes a one-two with Jackson before opening up his body and letting fly, the shot going well wide.

Another good chance for the hosts and it’s not shock to write that it’s come from the industry of Arribas on the right. He fires in a low cross that evades everyone in the box.

Estevao goes down in the box, it looks as though it could well be a penalty but the referee waves play on. The Brazilian is the shown a yellow card for possibly lashing out having not got the decision he wanted.

The hosts have asserted themselves well this half, in much the same way as they did in the first 45 minutes.

Another good chance for the hosts and again it’s all too easy as Zahedi is one-on-one with the keeper. The striker, however, dithers a bit too long and Slonina makes a fine save. JDT have had plenty of chances to add to their sole goal...

Chelsea have had a ragged start to this half.

Good work from JDT who keep the ball well in midfield before a throughball is played to the on-rushing Zahedi but Slonina comes out well.

They’re back under way in Johor, and there’s an early chance for Jackson who gets the ball in the box, but the ball gets stuck underneath him and he cannot get in a good attempt in on goal.

And that is the last action of an entertaining half. Chelsea started well before the hosts opened the scoring. JDT then took control of the half and should, if truth be told, have extended their lead. But Delap did well to earn the penalty that he subsequently scored and should have made it 2-1 with the last kick of the 45.

Worrying signs at the back, however, for Alonso. Will Chelsea go to four at the back after the break?

The answer to that question (see last post) was so very nearly yes...

Jackson plays in a peach of a through ball with the outside of his right foot, Delap is one-on-one with the keeper and looks for all the world as though he has to score. BUT he scuffs his shot wide.

There will be three minutes of added time. Can Chelsea head into the break with an unexpected lead?

Free-kick for Chelsea on the JDT byline. The ball is put deep into the box, it’s headed back by Tosin before the ball is blazed over the bar.

A minute later Tosin then let’s fly form 25 yards, the ball goes well over the bar.

The hosts should have been more than 1-0 to the good and now they’re drawing. Goals change matches...

Having won the penalty Delap fires the spotkick home, sending the keeper the the wrong way.

Penalty to Chelsea and it’s all thanks to good centre-forward play by Delap. He gets the ball in the box and Medina manhands him to the ground. The referee doesn’t hesitate before pointing to the spot.

Chelsea have struggled to create anything since the opening 15 minutes. They have no control at the front and none at the back currently.

As I type that JDT have another good chance to turn the 1-0 lead into a 2-0 lead. Arribas, whose been a menace all game, dances toward the Chelsea box before delaying the pass too long.

JDT are finding a lot of joy on the flanks, there are three at the back for Chelsea and on the outside are two youngsters. The hosts are working the space well.

Yet again Chelsea are made to look decidedly average. A simple ball over the top on the right opens up the visitors’ defence and Arribas is in on goal, he cuts in and lets fly with his left peg, the shot going wide.

That should have been 2-0 to the Malaysian powerhouses.

Worrying signs for Chelsea who have struggled to keep possession up top and looked vulnerable at the back.

Yet more good work from JDT who are being given space by Chelsea. Marcos Guilherme slaloms into the west Londoners’ box and Tosin again doesn’t look the most assured but the JDT player cuts the ball back and the visitors can clear the danger.

Another good attack from the hosts who get in a shot in on goal, it’s deflected and loops into the grateful arms of Sharman-Lowe in the Chelsea goal.

There’s a break in play with Anselmino down and suffering what looks like a hamstring injury. He is eventually replaced by Reggie Watson.

Meanwhile, the home fans are in fine voice and waving several HUGE flags.

Yep, everyone’s least favourite part of the World Cup in the U, S of A is back. To be fair it’s humid in Johor so taking on fluids during the first 45 minutes is no bad idea.

There’s a bit of argy-bargy not really what you should get in a ‘friendly’. There hasn’t been a bad chellenge in the match so far so not sure where that came from...

Yet more good work from the hosts, this time it’s down the right, Arribas getting the better of Anselmino before shooting at the near post - the attempt hitting the side netting.

After a lively start Chelsea have been second best.

Poor defending from the visitors there but the chance was well snapped up by JDT.

Lovely break from the hosts. They break down the left at pace, before the ball is threaded through to the back post and Arif Aiman sidefoots into the back of the net with aplomb.

So very nearly an opener for Chelsea. They break at pace thanks to Estevao who drives down the middle before playing in Jackson. The striker cuts in from the left and shoots, the attempt is saved well by Hamzi and Estevao’s follow up is wide. Is a goal coming?

Free-kick for Chelsea some 35 yards out. Too far fro a shot on goal? Of course it is. The ball is floated into the box and the visitors earn a corner.

What can they create from this set piece? ‘Not much’ is the initial answer as the ball is cleared by JDT but Chelsea win possession back and the ball is fed to Estevao on the left, the Brazilian goes for go with his trusty left peg but the bal goes high and wide.

JDT attack down the left, it’s a lovely ball in that forces a fine header to clear the danger from Adarabioyo.

No sooner had I sent that last post than Chelsea break through the middle. The ball is fed through to Delap who gets a left-footed shot in on goal forcing a good save from the JDT keeper Hamzi.

Quiet, low-key start to the match. No real shock there, it is a pre-season friendly.

JDT give the ball away in their half and Chelsea have a half-decent platform to launch an attack from. They cannot fashion a chance and also lose possession.

They’re under way in southern Malaysia, Chelsea are in their vibrant blue and the hosts are wearing a fetching pink number. There was a late change for the visitors, Mamadou Sarr has been replaced by Olutayo Subuloye.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE JOHOR: Sharman-Lowe; Sarr, Tosin, Anselmino; Quenda, Nicoll-Jazuli, Essugo (c), Gittens; Estevao; Jackson, Delap; subs: Slonina, Curd, Subuloye, Diakite, Watson, Mudryk, Walsh, Kavuma-McQueen, Satpayev

...Luis Garcia. The Spaniard has history with Chelsea, remember the ‘ghost goal’?

Arriving for duty! 🫡 pic.twitter.com/M2XEkLC18n

Your Chelsea side today! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/0OvvGVmgpc

A mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters you may not have heard of.

Johor Darul Ta’Zim – more commonly known as JDT – are the Man Utd of Malaysia (at least that’s according to a Malaysian friend of mine). In 2013, they were going nowhere and were the dictionary definition of a stagnant club, low on confidence and trophies. That was until the Crown Prince bought the club and, over the next 13 years, transformed it into the powerhouse it is today.

As if to underline JDT’s dominance over Malaysian football they are one game away from the world record unbeaten run in a top flight. The new season of the Malaysian Super League gets under way later this month and should they avoid defeat in their opening match they will extend their unbeaten run - which began in April 2021 - to 109 games and surpass the world record set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s.

Chelsea’s pre-season tour of South East Asia ends today with a match against Johor Darul Ta’zim in Malaysia. The clash comes barely 24 hours after the west Londoners beat AC Milan 3-0 in Jakarta, a much-needed win coming on the back of defeats against Juventus and Tottenham.

A fine volley from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to victory in the Indonesian capital.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head into the break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

Alonso’s side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto.

Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Today, the west London side face Malaysian powerhouses Johor at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium, more on them later, but considering the tight turnaround from yesterday’s match today’s clash will provide a stern test.

“The idea, with the game against Milan and then one in Johor, was to arrive at this weekend with players not being ready for 90 minutes until now,” Alonso explained after the win in Jakarta.

“We wanted to have a logical progression in their loads; so we had our plan and we’ve stuck to that.

“We have another idea [against Johor]; that was decided yesterday [Friday]. The idea is that many young players were coming to have chances to play tomorrow. If not, we’d have been short, as playing two games in two days is quite intense. So we will need them.”

#1606. De Rossi praises Genoa’s performance, Amorim as a head coach and Milan’s ‘world class’ duo

Daniele De Rossi has revealed that he congratulated his Genoa players despite their defeat against AC Milan this afternoon.

Milan did what they had to do after their midweek setback against Ferencvaros at San Siro by securing a much-needed three points to move back into the top four in the Serie A table, at least for the time being. It was not a given either, against a Genoa side who had won three in a row and four in five.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Both goals came in the first half as Alphadjo Cisse continued his excellent scoring form by firing in Adrien Rabiot’s cut-back. Christian Pulisic buried Goncalo Ramos’ square ball to double the advantage, and Ellertsson scored late to make it a tense finale, but Milan got over the line.

De Rossi was interviewed by DAZN (via MilanNews) after the full-time whistle at the Marassi to give his opinion on what was largely a positive performance from his side, but not the result to match.

Did you throw it away with individual mistakes?

“I congratulated my players. The performance was very good. I don’t like to talk about individual errors. I hear so many coaches talking about individual errors when they concede goals, not when they score. Kalulu also made an individual error on Baldanzi’s goal [against Juventus].

“That’s football. We can’t just rely on it when it suits us. There are ways to correct mistakes. We all made some mistakes collectively on the goals; we could have done better, but overall, I think the game was very good.”

It was an excellent reaction from the team despite going two behind…

“Before the last break, we were a bit more fragile, but my players always reacted. We were orderly in our reactions. Milan have a couple of players who hide the ball from you when it’s hot, but it never gets hot for them.

“They make you lose a bit of distance, and you have to put in a game that requires a lot of physical sacrifice. Everyone did it, and it makes me realise I have a team to be proud of. If we play like we did today, we’ll win more games than we’ll lose.”

“I shouldn’t judge him: he’s younger than me, but he has a lot more experience than me. I learn from him. We study him, we watch him. He plays with a system I really like.

“He puts a lot of quality on the wings, something I’ve also tried to do here. Certainly not Moreira’s level, but with the right proportions and possibilities.

“I like the way he communicate, he doesn’t blame his players even when they lose, he’s always honest when they lose. He’s doing an excellent job.”

“For anyone who loves this post, it’s exciting to see this player paint football like this at 41. Last season I had him man-marked, this season he played with two. He has more time on the ball.

“Maybe he goes a little slower, but the thought goes. We’ve clashed a couple of times and I told him, ‘I don’t play anymore so I can’t beat you’. But he’s beautiful, truly beautiful. He’s like Rabiot: world-class players.”

#1605. Arsenal transfer news: Julian Alvarez pursuit revived as Martin Zubimendi exit expected

By Alexis Pereira | 09 Nov 2026 20:55, Last updated: 09 Nov 2026 20:55

Arsenal’s pursuit of Atletico Madrid forward Julian Alvarez could be revived by the expected January departure of midfielder Martin Zubimendi, with the two deals reportedly linked, according to Spanish radio station RNE. The report, relayed by AS and Mundo Deportivo, suggests an attractive scenario for boss Mikel Arteta, but one that is far from certain to happen.

Zubimendi joined from Real Sociedad for around £60m (€70m) in the summer of 2025 and probably did not expect to find himself in this situation. Once regarded as an important part of Arteta’s plans, the Spain international has gradually lost ground in the pecking order, with competition in midfield from Declan Rice, Martin Odegaard, Mikel Merino and Bruno Guimaraes considerably reducing his chances to play.

His game time has been especially limited this season, with 380 minutes across 12 matches. That makes a January departure very likely unless something changes, and Atletico Madrid have reportedly moved to try to bring back a player admired by their sporting department for several years.

For boss Diego Simeone, the Basque midfielder would be a major addition. He has the qualities needed to set the tempo from a deep position, including passing, reading of space and the ability to cope with the opposition press. The two clubs still have to find common ground, however, as Arsenal made a substantial investment to sign him.

According to RNE’s Silvia Barba, the Argentina forward could be involved in discussions between Arsenal and Atletico. Arsenal like his profile and had already shown interest during the summer. The former Manchester City player’s situation in Madrid is delicate, with only two goals this season and a relationship that is sometimes strained with part of the home support.

Going from interest to a completed transfer is another matter, though. Atletico do not want to sell cheaply, and Mundo Deportivo mentions a very high figure of around £128m (€150m), an amount that is hard to imagine even for Arsenal, particularly in the January window, when the Madrid club would have to agree to part with a major player in the middle of the season.

Zubimendi’s exit could reshuffle the cards and make talks easier, but it does not guarantee an Alvarez deal. Arsenal may follow the situation, but they should not consider the Argentine’s arrival as imminent.

#1604. Why Enzo Maresca is sticking with 'awe-inspiring' Gianluigi Donnarumma despite Leipzig horror show, growing catalogue of errors and a worrying downward trend

Published: 12:00 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 07:07 EST, 6 November 2026

There was a Manchester City fan on Thursday’s Ryanair flight back home from Leipzig wearing a Gianluigi Donnarumma sticker on his coat, portraying the Italian as Don Vito Corleone. The sticker, a bit worn and a bit crumpled, was peeling off. A metaphor exists within that somewhere.

Tough times for Donnarumma, a calamitous night in the Champions League – beaten at his near post by Ridle Baku's cross for one goal, fumbling another routine effort at the feet of a striker and allowing a straightforward shot to squirm through his fingers – just adding to the feeling that the past few weeks have not reflected kindly on him.

Question marks around Donnarumma’s suitability between the sticks are becoming more pronounced after a catalogue of mistakes this season. One against Paris Saint-Germain when Maghnes Akliouche’s shot was too hot (some would argue two after neglecting his near post for Desire Doue’s opener) and then Nicolas Jackson shooting through him at Aston Villa last month.

Each time, Enzo Maresca has publicly recognised the errors and intimated that nobody needs to rake over them in detail with his No1, who is experienced enough to know he must do better.

Now Leipzig. ‘It’s not a concern,’ Maresca said of the latest gaffe. The manager’s defences of Donnarumma are racking up and what City are witnessing is fundamental problems from somebody described as the best the world has to offer.

Maresca has rejected the idea that summer signing Geronimo Rulli, a 34-year-old Argentina international, could take over the gloves, claiming that City line-ups are always ‘Gigio plus 10’. Rulli understood his lot when joining from Marseille, to feature in domestic cup competitions, and was happy with that.

Gianluigi Donnarumma had a night to forget in Leipzig this week, making at least three individual errors

But Man City boss Enzo Maresca will stand by his goalkeeper, claiming that City line-ups are always ‘Gigio plus 10’

Happy in a way that James Trafford was not, after making it clear that one season as Donnarumma’s understudy was not palatable.

He has flourished at Leeds United so far this season, leading to some observers criticising Hugo Viana for letting him go, only to blunder for a goal at Bournemouth last weekend. Worth remembering that it does happen to all of them at some point.

Trafford did not appear ready for the big time last year when starting the season ahead of the wantaway Ederson and City had their eyes on Donnarumma months before landing him – a £26million deal struck just as Ederson left for Fenerbahce.

Trafford will be ready soon and is pushing Jordan Pickford hard to be England's No1, but definitely wasn’t back then.

With Trafford gone and Maresca seemingly ruling out his No2 taking over – while also making a vague reference to taking stock over the international break – it appears that City would have no option but to stick with Donnarumma if they did actually want to bring about a change. January signings seem remote in the current climate of guilty verdicts and appeals.

But there is something outstanding that Donnarumma does offer, one that does set him apart. Maresca categorised the stunning one-handed save from Leipzig’s Christoph Baumgartner as one nobody else could make.

And while some hyperbole might be at play there, very few could lay claim to producing that kind of moment on a semi-regular basis.

Repelling Baumgartner is up there with Donnarumma’s instinctive save from Bryan Mbeumo at a crucial juncture on debut last year and thwarting Alexis Mac Allister in a victory at Anfield. The sort of awe-inspiring saves thousands pay money to witness.

Very few goalkeepers can claim to make wonder-saves as regularly as Donnarumma does

Donnarumma's impressive shot-stopping in the Premier League is evidenced by this graphic of every shot he has faced since joining City (red circles = goals, blank circles = saves)

Nobody across the Premier League has a higher save percentage than Donnarumma’s 71.5 since his arrival from PSG. More scientifically, only Bart Verbruggen and Senne Lammens have prevented more goals in that time – a metric measured by the xG of shots compared to how many goals were conceded.

Donnarumma has prevented seven goals (1.4 this season), with Brighton’s Verbruggen at 9.7 and Manchester United's Lammens at 8.1 across the same period. These are broadly encouraging numbers for City, despite Donnarumma's save percentage dipping to 69.7 this season – eighth among his peers, with Trafford way out in front on 79.5.

City will need to keep a careful eye on that downward trend from a 27-year-old who they brought to the club to act as the anchor, to bail them out in a way that Ederson struggled. That was the trade-off for his limited footwork, being incapable of playing through the opposition lines in a way the Brazilian could.

The wonder saves cancel all of that out. Donnarumma has been the goalkeeper’s goalkeeper for those alone. But were the certainty around that aspect of his game to waver on a longer-term basis, City should have decisions to make.

#1603. Michael Carrick latest: Man United's 'expected' sack decision revealed amid Mauricio Pochettino links

By Ben Sully | 09 Nov 2026 23:48

Manchester United are reportedly expected to sack Michael Carrick before the club's next game against Liverpool.

Carrick's fate appeared to be written on the wall when his side went 4-2 down in Sunday's Premier League home clash against Aston Villa.

However, his charges staged a late fightback to rescue a 4-4 draw at Old Trafford, giving something for the Man United decision-makers to think about as the Premier League pauses for the international break.

While the comeback proved the players were still willing to battle for Carrick, the reality is the club are languishing in the Premier League relegation zone after failing to win any of their last eight matches in the top flight.

The Man United hierarchy have ultimately been left to decide whether they have seen enough in the last two games against Roma and Aston Villa to allow Carrick to lead the team after the international window.

Man United's director of football Jason Wilcox is leading the review into Carrick's future, with the help of chief executive Omar Berrada, before co-owners Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family sign off the final decision.

According to The Athletic, the expectation is that Carrick will be relieved of his duties before the Red Devils return to action against Liverpool on November 22.

While Man United insist they are yet to make a final decision, the club are already working on potential replacements.

As a result, it appears that Carrick's tenure as Man United's permanent boss will end after overseeing just four wins in 16 matches this season.

The Athletic report claims that Mauricio Pochettino will feature 'highly' among the shortlist of potential managerial candidates.

Pochettino recently extended his contract with the USA national team until 2030, although he is said to have a release clause in his deal.

Eddie Howe is also said to be in the mix, although it was recently reported that Man United are not completely sold on the former Newcastle United boss.

Ex-Germany boss Julian Nagelsmann is another possible option if Man United officially decide to remove Carrick from his post.

#1602. Andoni Iraola: Liverpool cannot ‘sustain the level’ I want

Andoni Iraola has conceded that Liverpool cannot currently “sustain the level” he expects after his side squandered a two-goal lead for the second match in a row.

In the Spaniard’s first game at Anfield since becoming manager, Monaco fought back to win 3-2 by virtue of Paris Brunner’s late glancing header seven days on from Leeds United’s 4-2 victory in Chicago, emphasising Liverpool’s alarming lack of depth, particularly in defence.

“We played a good first half, especially a good 30 minutes. Right now we probably don’t have much more, in terms of the levels required to play like this. They deserved to turn around the game.

“We won the first two pre-season games, but the last two we cannot sustain the level we want for all of the game. As soon as we made some changes, players start to get tired and we cannot sustain that level. So, we have work to do.”

Alex on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/PT6AYrLxyz

Alisson, Virgil van Dijk and Cody Gakpo all made their first appearances and contributed to a lively first-half in which Iraola’s commitment to man-to-man marking and an intensive pressing structure were evident out of possession. With the ball in the first half they demonstrated the kind of slick passing that Bournemouth employed to carve opponents open on the counter-attack.

A nimble one-two between Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai allowed the Dutch midfielder to set up Alexander Isak to score with a shot from 16 yards and the most expensive player in English football history laid claim to the second, too, when he seemed to hook in a rebound from Lukas Hradecky’s save while lying in the six-yard box.

Later he would graciously acknowledge that he and Florian Wirtz had connected with the ball simultaneously and he was happy to yield the credit to his team-mate.

Our second goal of the game, scored by Wirtz… we think 🤔 pic.twitter.com/FUzA363Oxw

At that point it seemed that victory would be a cakewalk but just before half-time Aleksandr Golovin caught Van Dijk out with a feint and late swerve to the right, tripping over the Liverpool captain’s clumsy hack. Despite a heavy limp, Golovin hammered the penalty past Alisson’s dive to make it 2-1 at the break.

Iraola rationed his early changes at the start of the second half to two but Liverpool could not regain their rhythm and Mika Biereth capitalised on a Gravenberch error to score the equaliser after battling to be first to the rebound when Giorgi Mamardashvili saved his first effort, stroking his effort through Wataru Endo’s legs.

Cue five substitutions as soon as that goal had gone in and a raft more followed, killing the remaining half-hour of all momentum and cohesion. By the time Brunner exploited a dozy mix-up between Milos Kerkez and Federico Chiesa about whose responsibility he was at a corner to flash his header past Mamardashvili, only two of the 22 starters were still on the pitch.

Liverpool: Alisson (Mamardashvili 46), Tsimikas (Kerkez 59), Van Dijk (c) (Chambers 59), Ndukwe (Endo 46), Frimpong (Ramsay 75), Gravenberch (Nyoni 59), Gakpo (Ngumoha 59), Wirtz (McConnell 59), Koumas (Chiesa 75), Isak (Muñoz 59)Substitutes: Morrison, Davies.Goals: Isak (16), Wirtz (29)Monaco: Hradecky, Nazinho (Mawissa 75), Dier (c) (Kehrer 75), S Sané, Vanderson (Teze 46), Golovin (Idumbo 75), Cabral (Soubeir 75), Camara (Benzahra 64), Detourbet (Coulibaly 64), Biereth (Brunner 80), Abline (Konaté 64).Substitutes: Assab, Kohn, Lienard, Nibombe, Touré.  Goals: Golovin (44 pen), Biereth (56), Brunner (88)

They played well in the first half, as they did against Leeds, but lost all shape and structure in the second half to lose 3-2.

Yellow card for Konate for clattering into Endo late. That’s the last of the action.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 3 (Brunner)  Brilliant near-post glancing header from a devilishly whippy, dipping corner. Kerkez doing his best Rip van Winkle impression.

Diligent defensive work by Ngumoha stops Konate’s run down the outside left.

A final substitution, hopefully. Brunner replaces Biereth. Konate’s shot, a pearoller, is easily saved by Mamardashvili after A mix-up between Kerkez and Munoz.

As usual, the substitutions have killed the game. Watched Leeds vs RB Leipzig yesterday. They played two 60 minute matches which kept it more competitive for longer but still descended into a kickabout late on.

Mawissa, Kehrer, Idumbo and Soubeir have replaced Nazinho, Dier, Golovin and Cabral.

Monaco also made changes, four I think. Will catch up with then once they’re confirmed. Ramsey is into the game straight away tp stop Coulibaly’s shot.

Ramsay, Chiesa and Elliott are coming on for Szoboszlai, Frimpong and Koumas. Lovely applause for Elliott.

Konate sweeps a left-foot shot from the left of the box past the right post with Mamardashvili forced into a headlong dive. Liverpool have lost their defensive shape and intensity, allowing Monaco to punch holes through the lines with some direct running.

Nazinho gets round Frimpong down the Monaco left and cuts back the perfect pass to put it on a plate for Coulibaly who hammers a left-foot shot from the right of the D that Mamardashvili throws up his hands to block. That would have stung. Good save. A flag would have meant it wouldn’t have counted but even so Frimpong’s defensive work wasn’t good enough.

It’s been very scrappy since the changes but then Ngumoha pounces on to a loose ball, glides up the right and tries to play Koumas in behind the back four. Sadly, he overhits the pass which trickles out for a goal-kick. Cue an ovation and cries of ‘Rio! Rio!’

Three changes for Monaco with Detoubet, Abline and Camara departing for Benzhara, Coulibaly and Konaté.

Ngumoha has gone to the right wing and Koumas is playing through the middle as a false nine.

Liverpool make five changes with Gakpo, Van Dijk, Wirtz, Tsimikas and Isak departing while Munoz makes his ‘debut’ with Ngumoha, Nyoni, Chambers, McConell and Kerkez.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 2 (Biereth) Mistake by Gravenberch allows Golovin to play a pass into the left half of the box for Biereth. His first shot is well saved by Mamardashvili at full stretch but his tenacity allowed him to get to the rebound ahead of Endo, swivel and stick his second effort in to equalise.

Monaco overplay at the edge of the box, Detourbet, Biereth and Abline playing ‘after you. Claud’, instead of shooting.

A slick, short passing move between Gravenberch, Wirtz and Isak ends with Isak on the deck in the box after Gravenberch’s step-over allowed the ball to run to him. Isak took a touch to move the ball on to his left but gave the defender a glimmer of it and he hacked it away before felling Isak as well as collateral damage.

Quiet start to the half. Biereth just pressed Mamardashvili but the keeper managed to sweep the ball away even though under more pressure than he would have expected.

Liverpool try to play out from the back with Mamardashvili spearing a straight pass to Gravenberch who tried to knock it round the corner for Endo but the ball skidded under his studs and out for a throw-in.

Isak is apparently claiming both goals. Replays are indistinct. He could have clipped it in off his heel as he had a swing at the ball while grounded at the same time as Wirtz.

Our second goal of the game, scored by Wirtz… we think 🤔 pic.twitter.com/FUzA363Oxw

Endo has slotted in at centre-back alongside Van Dijk.

Half-time changes: Mamardashvili for Alisson and Endo for Ndukwe.

For Monaco, Teze for Vanderson at right-back.

Much to admire in that first-half performance from Liverpool’s front six and centre-backs, the latter two particularly out of possession and winning it back. The man-to-man system is working well for them. But they should be out of sight by now instead of leading by only a goal.

Liverpool free-kick on the right after a foul on Koumas. Szoboszlai whips in the cross and Van Dijk gets up first to the left of the penalty spot but bludgeons his header about a foot wide of the right post.

Charlie Adam says the penalty was ‘a soft one’ but Van Dijk did not adjust when Golovin shifted it to his right, stuck out a leg and Golovim understandably decided to topple over the hurdle.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 1 (Golovin, pen) Speared it into the top right. Alisson went the right way but was beaten for pace and power.

The referee, Jarred Gillett, gives Monaco a penalty. It was deserved, too. Golovin went on a driving run down the middle, shifted it to his right and was tripped by Van Dijk.

Liverpool are well worth their lead. They are streets ahead of Monaco.

A microcosm of the game so far: Liverpool pass goes astray, a player wins it back – this time Gakpo – by snapping into a tackle before laying it off to his left for the unmarked Tsimikas to skim a low shot about a foot wide of the left post from 25 yards.

Monaco have done very little since that wee salvo in the opening minute but just now Abline was given too much space from distance but whacked his shot into the Kop.

Big cheer from the crowd for Hugo Ekitike

The impressive Koumas diddles Nazinho with a Cruyff turn but then thumps his shot straight into Hradecky’s chest.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 0 (Wirtz) Pass chipped out to Koumas down the right who arcs a cross to the back post. Gakpo meets it with a header back across goal to Isak whose first effort from a couple of yards is blocked but the ball gets stuck under Isak’s falling body and Wirtz is Johnny on the Spot to stab it in from a 18 inches as Dier tried to scramble it away.

Liverpool have been impressive so far but if there has been a weakness it’s still the balance in central midfield defensively. Going forward both Gravenberch and Szobiszlai have dovetailed together well. They win the ball back when Van Dijk steps out and the midfield two fly forward to tee up Koumas for a shot that strikes Dier.

Chance for Wirtz, who opens his body from the left of the D to try to bend a shot into the bottom right corner but fizzes it the wrong side of the post.

It’s been pretty breathless since the goal, Liverpool dozily letting Monaco through the middle before twice cutting Monaco apart in midfield only for Isak to overrun a pass in the box delivered by Wirtz and then Koumas to shoot over.

Liverpool 1 Monaco 0 (Isak) Chip to Gakpo down the left of the box, he clips it first time back to Gravenberch in the D who lays it off to Szoboszlai. Ping-ping-ping. Szoboszlai keeps the tempo high with return, the one in the one-two with Gravenberch who picks out Isak to bury a shot from about 15 yards into the bottom left corner.

Alex on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/PT6AYrLxyz

Excellent move from Liverpool, instigated by Ndukwe’s fine tackle on Biereth. He knocks it short to Gravenberch who arrows a 60-yard pass out to Koumas hurtling down the right. He measures his cross perfectly for Gakpo stealing in off the left wing and though he connects powerfully with the meat of his brow, he bashes it straight at the keeper. He was offside in any case, it transpires.

Charlie Adam on co-comms points out that Liverpool are going man-to-man now in classic Iraola/Bielsa style and when the camera goes high you can see it, especially with the full-backs.

Liverpool are carving the middle of the park up with incisive passing. Szoboszlai starts a move that sends Isak down the left of the box. He traps the chip, turns back to face away from goal and taps a pass back to Wirtz who gallops on to it and bends a shot that Hradecky dives low to his left to beat away with a firm left wrist. Frimpong pounces on the rebound and clips a tame effort straight at Hradecky who had quickly restored himself to the vertical.

Van Dijk gobbles up a long pass over Ndukwe, snuffing out any possibility of Biereth getting there first.

Tsimikas is free down the left but overhits his cross on the run when Isak was begging for a cut-back. The left-back went for the back post and ballooned his centre behind, miles beyond Koumas and Wirtz.

Liverpool defend the corner solidly and Frimpong races away on the counter, bombing on to the ball and sprinting into the Monaco half. But his touch is not as sound as his pace and Monaco deal with him when he fluffs his control.

A period of applause in memory of Kevin Keegan ❤️ pic.twitter.com/AkPZG7babe

Liverpool kick off defending the Kop. They roll the ball back to Frimpong who chips a long pass up the right to Koumas who hares on to the pass down the right and crosses, just beyond Isak. Hradecky gathers and bowls the ball out. A mistake by Tisimikas lets Biereth barrel through the inside-right to hammer a shot that Alisson turns behind for a corner.

The crowd applauds in the modern way. My goodness he was a terrific player. Saw him play for Liverpool, Southampton and Newcastle. Absolutely relentless.

Virgil van Dijk has the pennant. Liverpool are wearing all red with the paint splashes of the 1990 kit. Monaco are in a very pale green.

For me it’s a special game, most of the players and people will be ‘it’s [just] a pre-season friendly’, but for me it’s a lot more than this. It will be the first time I have the chance to go out, to feel this stadium and I hope we can also perform well.

It’s a good game for us, because it’s going to be demanding, it’s a team that wants to dominate and they also want to press high so we will see how we are.

I think the cases of Ali[sson], Cody, and Virgil I think it’s their first game. It shouldn’t go longer than 45 minutes, maybe a little bit more if they feel comfortable.

Also for some of the others Ryan, Flo, and Alex, it’s the second game so we have to be aware of those things.

But the league starts in two weeks, so we cannot wait also too much; we have to give them quality minutes.

I think today is going to be a good reference, two games – Monaco and Como – teams that try dominate the game, they are very good in possession, so they will demand us the best without the ball. If we want to control the game and also physical teams, they are probably a very good test.

I hope we are at the level and we can do very good games.

Le 𝐗𝐈 qui débutera cette rencontre face à 𝐋𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐨𝐥 📋 pic.twitter.com/2cOYRbzUEN

🥳 Feliz aniversário, 𝐅𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐩𝐞 𝐋𝐮𝐢́𝐬! 🎉Notre coach fête aujourd'hui ses 41 ans 🎂 pic.twitter.com/VTd4BQ5rRK

Alisson, Van Dijk and Gakpo return, Ndukwe continues in defence.

The Reds to take on AS Monaco at Anfield!Watch the match LIVE on All Red Video 📺

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the first of two Liverpool home friendlies after their preseason tour of the United States. Andoni Iraola’s side saw off Wrexham and Sunderland in their first two matches but gave away a two-goal lead at half-time in the final fixture and ended up being beaten 4-2 by Leeds United in Chicago in the last game after multiple changes. What did we learn? Not a huge amount in the absence of Virgil van Dijk, Alisson, Víctor Muñoz, Cody Gakpo and Alexis Mac Allister, the first four of whom are available today other than an ongoing vulnerability from set-pieces and Curtis Jones looking like he is in desperate need of a fresh start.

This afternoon at Anfield they take on AS Monaco who finished seventh in Ligue 1 this season but are under new management with the recruitment of the former Chelsea and Atlético left-back Filipe Luís as head coach. It’s quite the coup for Le Rocher given he led Flamengo to their first Brazilian title in five years, the Copa Libertadores and the Copa do Brasil in his 18 months in charge.

In pre-season so far he has overseen a 5-2 win over fourth-tier AS Saint-Priest, a 2-0 defeat by Sporting Clube, a 2-2 draw with Cercle Bruges and a 1-0 victory over Getafe. They have sold their best player, Maghnes Akliouche, to PSG for £43m and Aladji Bamba to Newcastle for £34m but have so far retained Mamadou Coulibaly and Folarin Balogun, signed and made Ansu Fati’s loan move into a long-term deal.

Iraola may well persevere with Trey Nyoni in midfield who, after his performances on tour, ought to be on the threshold of a breakthrough season and it would be interesting to see him paired with Ryan Gravenberch just behind Dominik Szoboszlai.

Ifeanyi Ndukwe, who played well in America after coming on for the injured Joe Gomez, does not have a UK work permit and will have to go abroad on loan for the season but Jérémy Jacquet, who has yet to feature, was due to have a fitness test this morning and would be a welcome to boost to a squad whose defence still requires significant reinforcements.

#1601. Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9,10,11,12,13. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

The capacity of cancer cells to switch phenotypic states, also called cellular plasticity, is a hallmark of cancer and is involved in tumour initiation and progression, including therapeutic resistance1. Glioblastoma (GB), the most common primary brain tumour in adults, is characterized by profound cellular heterogeneity and a dismal prognosis2,3. Although the genomic landscape of GB has been catalogued extensively, actionable genetic drivers remain scarce, and clinical responses to targeted therapies have been minimal4,5,6. Longitudinal studies have underscored the limited contribution of therapy-induced genetic evolution in GB and revealed remarkable clonal stability despite treatment7,8, suggesting that non-genetic mechanisms, such as epigenetic plasticity and transcriptional reprogramming, are central to adaptation and treatment resistance in GB. Seminal single-cell transcriptomic studies have shown that malignant GB cells occupy a continuum of cellular states resembling developmental progenitors (for example, oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC)-like and neural progenitor cell (NPC)-like), as well as astrocytic and mesenchymal-like phenotypes9,10. Patient-derived xenograft models have demonstrated that individual GB cells can give rise to multiple states, implying substantial plasticity10,11. However, whether these state transitions follow stereotyped routes or variable trajectories12,13, and how gene-regulatory mechanisms promote or constrain them, remain poorly understood.

Here, and in a companion study14, we address these questions by integrating single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and chromatin accessibility (single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing; snATAC-seq) profiles from more than one million cells from isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wild-type primary GBs. Using a computational approach (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference; scDORI) and systematic transcription factor (TF) perturbations, we decode enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks (eGRNs) at single-cell resolution and map the regulatory landscape that underlies the identity and plasticity of GB cells. Specifically, we model the gene-regulatory processes that govern GB cell states, identify key transcriptional regulators for each state, elucidate their roles in driving cell-state conversions and reconstruct a hierarchical roadmap of GB transitions. Our analyses reveal a structured landscape of GB state transitions shaped by epigenetic ‘highways’ and ‘barriers’. Neuronal-like cells emerge as a constrained, low-plasticity state stabilized by a network of transcriptional repressors that actively silences alternative malignant fates. We identify MYT1L as the key repressor in this network: gain-of-function of MYT1L restricts plasticity and induces a neuronal-like identity in patient-derived GB cells, and reduces tumour growth after transplantation in mice; by contrast, removal of MYT1L enhances plasticity and malignant features. These findings suggest that enforcing repressive barriers could lock GB cells into less adaptive states, and identify plasticity restriction as a potential therapeutic strategy.

Together with our companion study mapping spatio-temporal trajectories in GB tumours14, our findings reveal a conserved, epigenetically controlled hierarchy of cell states and transition routes in GB. Our work establishes transcriptional repressors as key suppressors of plasticity and underscores the potential of targeting the epigenetic foundations of state switching in brain cancer.

To characterize the regulatory landscape of GB, we generated a multiome snRNA–snATAC-seq atlas (see the companion study14), spanning parallel gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility profiles of more than one million cells collected across multiple sites (4–15) from 12 IDH-wild-type primary GB tumours, including peritumoral regions. In line with previous studies10, malignant GB cells exhibited vastly heterogeneous transcriptional profiles, ranging from developmental-like (OPC-NPC-like, OPC-like, OPC-neuronal-like, NPC-neuronal-like and astrocyte (AC)-progenitor-like) to glial injury response and hypoxia-associated (AC-gliosis-like, gliosis-like and hypoxia) phenotypes, as well as cycling signatures (proliferative) (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a).

A linear classifier trained on gene expression to predict transcriptional states is applied to gene accessibility profiles, with ambiguity of predictions indicating epigenetic plasticity. c, Epigenetic plasticity score determined using the approach in b, visualized for all cells on the UMAP plot in a. High scores denote high epigenetic plasticity. d, Confusion matrix for the accessibility-based predictions from the classifier in b: state prediction probability on the basis of gene accessibility profiles (rows), averaged across cells from each transcriptionally defined state (columns). First, we investigated the epigenetic plasticity of GB cells, assuming that accessible gene regions without active transcription indicate epigenetic plasticity. Inspired by a previous study15, we quantified how well accessibility profiles of cell-state markers predict transcriptionally defined cell states (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1b,c, Supplementary Table 1 and Methods). Cells whose chromatin profiles yield uncertain predictions are scored as more epigenetically plastic. Our analysis revealed that malignant cells exhibit greater epigenetic plasticity than non-malignant tumour microenvironment (TME) cells and analogous neurodevelopmental cell types (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1d–f), with chromatin accessibility in malignant cells often being compatible with multiple cell states (Fig. 1d). However, the extent of this plasticity varied significantly across GB cell states (Fig. 1e), and NPC-neuronal-like and OPC-neuronal-like cells stood out as the least plastic states. The variations in epigenetic plasticity could not be explained by differences in global coupling between gene expression and accessibility, were robust to differences in cell numbers per state and were consistently observed across patients (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1g–j). These data suggest that specific regulatory mechanisms underlie GB plasticity and govern cell-state heterogeneity.

To determine the specific gene-regulatory processes that underlie the observed differences in epigenetic plasticity, we aimed to identify relevant TFs, cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and their interplay across GB states using eGRNs. Established eGRN inference methods are not designed for the heterogeneity of a single-cell tumour atlas like ours16,17,18,19,20,21,22. Specifically, existing methods assume discrete, predefined cell-types and therefore cannot capture the continuous, cell-state-specific variation in eGRNs that defines malignant heterogeneity. Many also scale poorly to datasets of this size23. Moreover, previous methods focus mainly on signatures of transcriptional activation, despite the growing recognition of gene repression as a key regulator of cell identity and plasticity in cancer24,25.

To address these limitations, we developed scDORI, a computational approach for inferring continuous eGRNs and their relationships across cell populations using single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and scATAC-seq multiome data (Fig. 2a and Methods). Building on autoencoders26, scDORI performs joint dimensionality reduction of gene expression and chromatin accessibility profiles, decomposing both into gene-regulatory modules16,27,28,29,30,31,32 that are hereafter referred to as ‘Topics’. Each scDORI Topic encodes an eGRN in which TFs bind to CREs to control target gene expression, so the factors carry regulatory meaning rather than describing co-variation alone (Fig. 2a). Coupled decoders enforce this structure through established eGRN signatures: peak co-accessibility, TF chromatin binding, CRE–gene linkages and TF–target expression correlations that distinguish activation from repression16,17,18,19,20,21,22 (Extended Data Fig. 2a). By modelling each cell as a mixture of Topics, scDORI can capture continuous variations in eGRNs across cell states, without relying on predefined annotations. Conversely, a single Topic can be active across multiple cell states, enabling the identification of shared aspects of gene regulation. scDORI scales to datasets comprising millions of cells, and performs favourably, compared with existing eGRN inference methods, on benchmarks such as the prediction of enhancer–gene links33 (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c).

Auxiliary decoders impose mechanistic constraints from peak co-accessibility, TF binding, CRE–gene linkages and TF–target expression correlations that separate activation from repression. b, Activity of selected Topics in malignant cells, visualized on the UMAP representation from Fig. 1a. c, Heat map with hierarchical clustering of selected Topic activation patterns across GB states, revealing an activation continuum. Applied to our GB atlas, scDORI identified 31 active Topics with distinct patterns of activity across cells and patients (Fig. 2b,c, Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 2), each capturing co-accessible chromatin regions that were cis-linked to co-expressed genes (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Notably, the mechanistic constraints came at no cost to descriptive power: scDORI Topics explained transcriptional variation in tumour cells as well as or better than conventional dimensionality reduction methods did18,29 (Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). Clustering transcriptional GB states according to Topic activity patterns revealed four major regulatory states alongside a distinct proliferative (cycling) population, including developmental states (neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like) and AC–gliosis–hypoxia states (AC-like and gliosis–hypoxia) (Fig. 2c). Topics specific to individual states reflected gene programs that are characteristic of their developmental counterparts, such as neurotransmitter release in neuronal-like cells (Topic 37), PDGF signalling in OPC-NPC-like cells (Topic 34) and calcium ion homeostasis in AC-like cells (Topic 20)34,35,36 (Fig. 2e, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 2). These programs were also active in corresponding TME cell types, consistent with tumour cells co-opting developmental pathways.

As well as explaining differences between GB states, scDORI resolved functional heterogeneity within individual malignant states. For instance, in gliosis–hypoxia cells, distinct Topics captured hallmark features such as hypoxic stress (Topic 11), cytokine signalling (Topic 19) and vascular wound healing (Topic 12)37,38,39 (Fig. 2e). scDORI also identified ‘inter-state’ Topics (7, 9, 25, 29, 33, 36 and 49) that span several GB states. Most of these were enriched for programs linked to fate commitment and differentiation, indicating a potential role in mediating state transitions (Fig. 2c,e and Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Finally, scDORI identified Topics that were broadly active across most tumour cells, reflecting tumour-wide programs, such as inflammatory response (Topic 31) and cell adhesion (Topic 18)40 (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). The inferred Topics were reproducible across model restarts, consistently represented across patients with GB and transferable to independent single-cell GB atlases10 (Extended Data Figs. 3c and 4d–f). Notably, scDORI Topic-specific eGRNs accurately captured differential expression between GB cell states of these independent atlases (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h).

The eGRN encoded by each Topic directly yielded Topic regulators (TRs), defined as the TFs with the strongest predicted activation of the Topic-specific gene program. On average, scDORI identified about nine TRs per Topic (Fig. 2f, Supplementary Table 2 and Methods). These included known GB cell-state markers, such as ASCL1 in OPC-NPC-like cells (Topic 36), SOX11 in neuronal-like cells (Topic 24) and FOSL1 in gliosis–hypoxia cells (Topic 19), as well as TFs associated with the respective Topic programs, such as hypoxia (NFKB1, Topic 19) and stress response (JUND, Topic 11)10,41,42,43,44. State-specific TRs included lineage-specific TFs, such as SOX6 (Topic 34, OPCs) and TRPS1 (Topic 9, ACs), further supporting the idea that GB cells reuse developmental TFs and gene programs45,46,47. Besides positive regulation, scDORI-inferred repressive links and identified Topic safeguards (TSs): TFs that regulate an identity by silencing gene programs of states distinct from their state of activity; that is, alternative states (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Table 2 and Methods). For instance, ST18 and SOX10 emerged as putative repressors of alternative state programs in neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like programs, respectively. Several TSs also act as TRs of their own Topic, revealing factors that both activate their own identity program and repress those of alternative states. Collectively, scDORI redefines GB heterogeneity from a gene-regulation standpoint and reveals state-specific activators and repressors, many of which have not yet been described in GB.

The extent to which GB state transitions follow defined regulatory rules, and which TFs drive them, remain central questions in GB biology9,10. We reasoned that if scDORI faithfully captures these processes, then activating the predicted regulators should induce the associated cell states. To test this, we performed a pooled single-cell lentiviral overexpression (OE) screen of 55 TR and TS candidates across three patient-derived GB cell (PDGC) lines, co-cultured with primary cortical cells to provide a neural microenvironment (Fig. 3a, Extended Data Fig. 5, Supplementary Table 3 and Methods).

After quality control, we recovered 261,566 cells, with 54 of 55 candidate regulators showing robust and balanced induction (at least 100 cells captured with more than 1.5-fold change) across all three lines (Fig. 3b, Extended Data Fig. 5a–d and Supplementary Table 3). We used logistic regression models trained on the patient atlas to assign cell state and Topic identity to each screened cell, revealing perturbation-induced shifts (Supplementary Table 3 and Methods). Two-thirds of candidates induced state changes consistent with scDORI predictions, spanning both TRs (for example, SOX4, ASCL1, MEOX2 and EPAS1) and TSs (for example, ST18, RBPJ, ETV1 and FOSL1) (Fig. 3b). Perturbation effects were also mostly concordant across all three patient lines, despite their distinct baseline cell-state compositions (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 5e). Top-ranked regulators as predicted by scDORI induced their target states most strongly, particularly those of neuronal-like and AC-like states (Extended Data Fig. 5f). Performing the same analysis at the more granular Topic level, we confirmed that regulators from nearly all Topics induced their respective Topic programs, even when their gain of function was not sufficient to induce a full state conversion (for example, ESR2, BCL6 and NR3C2) (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). A notable exception was regulators of hypoxia-response Topics 11 and 12, which are likely to require extrinsic hypoxic signals for complete activation. Overall, 76% of tested regulators showed identity shifts consistent with our predictions at either the Topic or the state level (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 5h).

We defined high-confidence drivers for each of the four core GB states, combining three experimental lines of evidence: the strength of state change; the enrichment of the state gene signature after TF gain of function; and the dependence of state conversion on TF dose (Fig. 3d, Extended Data Fig. 5i,j and Supplementary Table 3). We then asked whether these regulators were also among the top-ranking scDORI predictions. We found that 81% (25 out of 31) ranked among the top predicted regulators of the corresponding state-associated Topics (Fig. 3d). Notably, scDORI also resolved distinct mechanisms of action among these drivers: some mainly activated state marker genes (MEOX2, PRRX1 and JUN), others repressed alternative-state marker genes (MYT1L, ST18 and SOX10), and a subset combined both modes (SOX4, FOXO1 and CEBPD) (Fig. 3d). Together, these results show that scDORI accurately nominates functional regulators of GB identity, and that their activation is sufficient to trigger corresponding state-specific transcriptional programs.

Having established that individual scDORI-predicted regulators can drive GB state transitions, we asked whether their endogenous expression and accessibility could explain how these transitions arise in patients. Examining each state’s TRs in cells of alternative states, we found that 39% (34 out of 87) were already expressed in at least one alternative state, whereas 68% (59 out of 87) were chromatin-accessible but transcriptionally silent, suggesting epigenetic priming for specific state transitions (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b).

To quantify primed transitions systematically, we computed a Topic activation potential (TAP) for each pair of Topics—an estimate of how readily cells in a source Topic can activate the TRs of a target Topic and mediate an identity shift. TAP scores integrate three components: the regulatory links from source-Topic TFs onto target-Topic TRs; the accessibility of those target TRs in source-Topic cells; and the importance of each TR in the target Topic (Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 6c–f, Supplementary Table 4 and Methods). TAP scores revealed a structured and markedly asymmetrical landscape of transitions between GB states (Fig. 4b). Inter-state Topics (33, 36 and 49) acted as connectivity hubs linking multiple states, consistent with their enrichment for fate-change signatures (Fig. 2e). By contrast, state-specific Topics differed sharply: OPC-NPC-like (34) and AC-like (9, 20 and 44) Topics showed strong TAP connections to multiple alternative states, whereas connections from neuronal-like (24, 37 and 41) and gliosis–hypoxia (11, 12 and 19) Topics were mainly confined within their own state (Fig. 4b,e). Together, these results highlight how the regulatory architecture and epigenetic priming of each state jointly determine its permissiveness to transition (Extended Data Fig. 6d–f).

The overall low transition potential of neuronal-like and gliosis–hypoxia Topics raised the question of whether these states are deprived of activating cues or actively constrained by repression. We therefore defined an analogous Topic repression score (TRS), mirroring TAP but built from the inverse signals: the repressive links from source-Topic TFs onto target-Topic TRs and epigenetic inaccessibility of those TRs in source-Topic cells (Fig. 4c, Extended Data Fig. 6g, Supplementary Table 4 and Methods). Neuronal-like Topics (24 and 37) showed the most widespread repression of alternative state Topics and marker genes, attributable to the aggregated activity of several neuronal-like TFs (Fig. 4d,e, Extended Data Fig. 6h,i and Supplementary Table 4). By contrast, other Topics showed either state-restricted repression (2, 20 and 36) or minimal repression overall (9 and 44) (Fig. 4d,e and Supplementary Table 4). Total Topic-level repression negatively correlated with the epigenetic plasticity of associated cells (Figs. 1e and 4f), further supporting a role for repression as an active barrier to state transitions.

To assess how activation and repression jointly shape transitions, we defined a net transition potential as the difference between TAP and TRS (Extended Data Fig. 6j,k). Aggregation at the state level revealed a hierarchy of transition potentials and barriers, consistent with the epigenetic plasticity of the respective states (Fig. 4f–h and Supplementary Table 4). OPC-NPC-like and AC-like states showed predominantly activating interactions towards other states, reflecting broad permissiveness to transitions, whereas neuronal-like and gliosis–hypoxia cells showed limited activation and, in the case of neuronal-like cells, predominant repression towards alternative states (Fig. 4g,h and Extended Data Fig. 6j,k). These interactions were often asymmetrical, pointing to preferential, directional routes of state change.

We next asked how this landscape compares with normal development, applying the same analysis to the developing human dorsal telencephalon48. There, transitions remained confined within neurogenic and gliogenic lineages, confirming that the model recovers established lineage relationships49,50,51,52 (Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 5). GB, by contrast, permits transitions across these lineage boundaries, identifying its expanded transition potential as an aberrant feature of malignancy rather than a rewiring of normal developmental hierarchies. Together, these results define a structured, asymmetrical transition landscape, jointly shaped by activation and repression, that qualitatively diverges from normal lineage programs.

Because we derived the transition landscape from profiles of dissociated cells, we wanted to find out to what extent this intrinsic logic could explain tumour organization in space and time. We therefore investigated the relationship between transition potentials and the spatial and temporal co-activity of Topic pairs in orthogonally derived data. In 97 matched spatial transcriptomics tumour sections (338,481 Visium spots)14, cross-state Topic pairs with a high transition potential (for example, Topics 9–25, 44–34 and 9–19) were more frequently co-active in the same regions than were pairs with weak or repressive links (for example, Topics 24–12, 24–2 and 37–44) (Pearson r = 0.488, P = 2 × 10−6, n = 84 pairs; Fig. 4i, Extended Data Fig. 8a–c and Supplementary Table 6). Across 57 pseudotemporally ordered clonal populations14, pairs with a high transition potential likewise showed stronger temporal co-activity (Pearson r = 0.466, P = 8 × 10−6, n = 84 pairs; Fig. 4j, Extended Data Fig. 8d–f and Supplementary Table 7). Transition potentials derived from Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs aligned more closely with both spatio-temporal patterns and epigenetic plasticity than did those from a single network averaged across Topics or eGRNs from alternative methods, showing the advantages of continuous, Topic-resolved modelling (Extended Data Fig. 8g–i). Although spatial and temporal co-activity alone cannot establish direct transitions, their convergence with the regulatory predictions supports the inferred GB transition roadmap. Together, these findings support a revised model of GB plasticity in which structured regulatory relationships both enable and restrict cell-state transitions, revealing potentially targetable effectors of malignant state change.

Increased cellular plasticity is likely to contribute to tumour progression and therapy resistance in GB53,54. Our transition analysis identified neuronal-like cells as the least plastic GB state, stabilized by transcriptional repression. We therefore asked whether neuronal-like regulators could be harnessed to restrict GB plasticity.

To this end, we profiled chromatin accessibility and transcriptional changes after gain of function of ten candidate TFs in PDGCs, comprising both predicted safeguard repressors (BCL11B, NR3C2, MYT1L, ST18, POU2F2 and BACH2) and activators of neuronal-like programs (SOX11, SOX4, ASCL1 and PBX1) (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). All candidate TFs induced specific regulatory changes consistent with scDORI predictions (Fig. 5a–c), and the predictions of differentially regulated genes were more accurate than were those of other eGRN methods (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Notably, all repressors silenced non-neuronal-like state programs at both the chromatin and the transcriptional level, whereas activators predominantly induced neuronal-like gene expression (Fig. 5a–c and Extended Data Fig. 9e). Although activator-driven identity induction modestly suppressed alternative states, repressor-driven chromatin closure was substantially better at constraining other cell fates, indicating that repression restricts plasticity more effectively.
